speechtext: Mr. WALTER SCOTT (West Assiniboia) moved for leave to introduce a Bill to amend the Mounted Police Pension Act, 1899. He said : Mr. Speaker, in moving for leave to introduce this Bill at this time I recognize that unless the government agree to put it on the Order paper as a government Bill, it is absolutely impossible to make any progress with it. I may explain that the intent of the amendment is to put the noncommissioned officers and men of the mounted police force in the same position as regards the calculation of their pensions as the officers are put in by the measure adopted by the House last session. At the present time the pensions of the non-commissioned officers and men of the force are calculated upon their average pay for three years preceding their retirement. By the Officers' Pension Act put through last year, the officers' pensions are now calculated up-
on their pay and allowances at the moment [DOT]of their retirement.
The same rule should apply to the men of the force.

I think so. I think the House will agree that the non-commissioned officers and men should occupy the same position in that respect as the officers. It is entirely unnecessary for me or anybody else to praise the mounted police force. Their services are recognized

I rise to a point of order. This appears to be a Bill to amend the Pension Act of the Mounted Police Force. The hon. member has no right to introduce a Bill of that kind. It must be introduced by a member of the cabinet, by resolution and with the consent of the Crown.
It is difficult for me to decide just now whether this is a money Bill or not.
It is, from the statement the hon. gentleman has made, to increase the pensions of the mounted police.
What I am really doing is urging that the government should take up this proposition.
I understand that the hon. member is moving to increase the pensions ?
That would certainly be the effect of the amendment.

As my hon. friend has already stated, the object he has in view is that the government should take charge of this Bill. The point taken by my hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is certainly well taken. I may say to my hon. friend that at this late stage of the session it is impossible for us to take up any more legislation than we have ; but the point to which he has called the attention of the House is engaging the attention of the government at the present time.
The matter dropped.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 259) to amend the North-west Territories Act.-The Minister of Justice.
Mr. SCOTT moved to add the following clause to the Bill:
Notwithstanding anything in the North-west Territories Act, or any Act in amendment thereto, the legislative assembly may, by ordinance, repeal the provisions of sections 49, 51, 53, 55, 64, 88, 89 and 90 of the said North-west Territories Act as amended and re-enacted the said provisions or substitute other provisions in lieu thereof, but nothing in this section contained shall be construed as giving to the legislative assembly power to pass ordinances for the con-
constitution, organization or maintenance of courts of criminal jurisdiction, or respecting procedure in criminal matters.

The effect would be to confer on the North-west assembly power to regulate all matters connected with the civil jurisdiction of the province. That is to say, they may determine the sittings of the court, the places where the court is to sit, how often it is to sit ; they may provide for the sittings of the court in banc or with a single judge; provide for the division of the territory into judicial districts ; define the territorial jurisdiction of the judges, and so on-all matters relating to the civil organization of the court. I think it is a step in the right direction.

Amendment agreed to.
Mr. SCOTT moved to add the following clause to the Bill:
Notwithstanding anything in the Northwest Territories Act, or any Act In amendment thereof, the legislative assembly may, by ordinance, repeal the provisions of sections 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 of chapteT 19 of the statutes of 1888, and section 18 of chapter 17 of the statutes of 1894, as that section is enacted by section 9 of chapter 28 of the statutes of 1897, and re-enact the said provisions or substitute other provisions in lieu thereof.

This amendment seems objectionable, not necessarily in the subject-matter, but in that it gives a local legislature power to repeal sections of a statute passed by this parliament. There must surely be some more logical way to get it than that. It would hardly be dignified for us to confer that power.

I would draw to tlie attention of my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley) the fact that paragraph 4, now under consideration, has reference to the organization of the North-west council itself, as the other paragraph we have been discussing has reference to the organization of the courts. Now, if we repeal the provisions and merely give authority to the North-west council to make others, we leave an interregnum during which some embarrassing conditions might arise. By this amendment we, in effect, say that in all matters affecting the North-west assembly, that body shall have the right either to adopt what we have done or to repeal the enactments which we have passed, and substitute others. My bon. friend will see the difficulty of adopting any other course.
I see, but still it seems that there ought to be some other way than to give power to the local legislature to repeal our enactments.
It is a little off the line, but my hon. friend will see that It is not unconstitutional.

I take it for granted that we have the power to delegate our authority. It is not so much the thing Itself

as the mode of doing it that I call attention

The difficulty that my hon. friend suggests occurred to my mind also, but it seems there is no relief. Suppose that these provisions were repealed. The North-west council may not sit for months yet. Should a by-election occur in the meantime, how is it to be provided for ? It seemed to me better to maintain the statute in these matters and simply give the legislature power to provide for the changes necessary.
Has the hon. minister's department considered this and come to the *conclusion that this is the only way in which it can be done ?
That is our view-this is the only way to avoid a hiatus.

Amendment agreed to.
Bill, as amended, reported; read the third time, and passed.

The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved that the House concur in the amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 243) to amend the Supreme and Exchequer Courts Act, the Exchequer Court Act, and the Act respecting the Judges of Provincial Courts. He said : There are two amendments to this Bill. As to the first of them, it relates to section 2 of the Bill as passed by this House. That section provided as follows :-
2. If any judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, or of the Exchequer Court of Canada, or of a Superior Court of any of the provinces of Canada resigns or has heretofore resigned his office as such judge to accept the office of lieutenant governor of a province, and if he serves or has served as 3uch lieutenant governor, and is not otherwise eligible for any retiring annuity as such judge, His Majesty may, at any time after tne expiration of the term of service of such judge as lieutenant governor, grant to such judge an annuity equal to two-thirds of the salary annexed to the judicial office which he held at the time of his resignation, to commence immediately upon the issue of such letters patent, and to continue thenceforth during his natural life.
This has been eliminated from the Bill.
What is the practical effect of the amendment 1

At the present time, a judge can withdraw after fifteen years of service and is entitled to a pension. The present object of the Bill in addition to this was that, when a judge has reached a certain limit of age he should be entitled to a full pension. After fifteen years, he receives a pension of two-thirds of his salary, and after thirty years of service, he is
entitled to withdraw with a pension equal to his whole salary. The amendment under this clause was that if the judge was appointed lieutenant governor before he became entitled to his full pension, at the expiration of his term of five years as lieutenant governor, he would be entitled to his pension as a judge. This has been eliminated by the Senate, as it was thought to be an interference with the independence of the judiciary, and we concur.
Are there any judges whom it affects ?
I do not know of any now.

I would draw the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister to the fact that this is a money Bill. The right belongs to this House to initiate, by resolution, and with the consent of the Crown, all Bills that provide for granting or using money belonging to the country, or imposing taxes or duties. In accordance with their rights, this House passed this Bill. The Bill was sent to the Senate, and has been by them amended. As I understand the constitutional rights of the two branches of the legislature, the Senate has no right to amend a money Bill, In amending this Bill, they have assumed a right which constitutionally they do not possess to amend a money Bill. I would ask the right hon. Prime Minister if he is not prepared, with his government, to defend the rights of the Commons, the elective chamber, which, undoubtedly has the right to deal with money Bills. When that question was being discussed in the other House, the first question raised was whether this was or was not a money Bill. I think that was completely settled by the authorities that was cited. First, it is a Bill dealing with pensions, which pensions are to be paid out of consolidated revenue. It provides for the using of a certain portion of the public revenue. It is. therefore, clearly a money Bill. The next question was raised, what is a money Bill. Edwin Gordon Blackmore's ' Procedure of the Legislative Council of South Australia,' nt pages 172 and 182, says :
A Bill introduced by a resolution of the House on the report of the Committee of the House, is a money Bill.
May says, speaking of this class of Bills ;
It follows accordingly that the Lords may not amend the provisions in Bills which they receive from the committees, dealing with the above mentioned subjects, so as to alter, whether by Increase or reduction, the amount of a vote or charge.
Todd says :
Money Bills are of three kinds : tax Bills, Bills of supply and Bills of appropriation.
Bourinot says, on page 585 of his second edition :
As a general rule, public Bills may originate in either House, but whenever they grant sup-

plies of any kind, or involve directly or indirectly the levying or appropriation of any tax upon the people, they must be initiated In the popular branch, in accordance with law and English constitutional practice. Section 53 of the British North America Act, 1867, expressly provides :
Bills for appropriating any part of the public revenue, or for imposing any tax or impost, shall originite in the House of Commons.
And a standing order of the House of Commons declares explicitly :
All aids and supplies granted to Her Majesty by the parliament of Canada are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all Bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the House, as it is the undoubted right of the House to direct, limit, and appoint in all such Bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the Senate.
But the iSenate alters them here by striking out one important clause, which provides for the appropriating of a certain amount of money. I draw the attention of the Prime Minister to this matter, and ask him if he is prepared to abandon the undoubted constitutional right of the House of Commons to control these Bills, and if he is prepared to accept the position taken by the Senate that they have a right to amend these money Bills.

There is no doubt that under our constitution as it has come down to us through the ages during which it has been formed, the granting of supplies in any form whatever is exclusively the privilege of the Commons, and all legislation, whether to levy or expend revenue, has to be originated in the Commons and cannot be altered in the upper chamber. But the question is :	What is a money
Bill ? if does not follow that every Bill which leaves this House which provides either for levying or expending revenue, is a money Bill. A money Bill has no special meaning in parliamentary language, and there is very little legislation which leaves this House which does not indirectly involve the granting of money, and in which therefore the privilege of the other branch of the legislature to exercise its powers of supervision could not be exercised if the hon. gentleman's doctrine were to prevail. The practice has been well understood, and we look to that to find a definition of a money Bill. A money Bill is, in its more restricted sense, a Supply Bill. Todd, which my hon. friend quoted a moment ago, gives an answer to the very question the hon. gentleman brings up, for Todd says on page 815 of the last edition of the first volume :
We will now proceed to consider the subject of money Bills, which are of three kinds, viz., tax Bills, Bills of supply, and Bills of appropriation. All these Bills have a peculiar form of preamble, which intimates that the revenue or grant of money is the peculiar gift of the House of Commons, and such Bills are invariably presented for the royal assent by the Speaker of the House of Commons.

This is what is understood by a money Bill, it is a Bill presented by parliament for the royal assent. To ascertain its character you have only to refer to an appropriation Act of any one year, and you will find that our practice conforms exactly to the rule laid down by Todd, namely, that the Supply Bill, which is a money Bill in the sense affirmed a moment ago by my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) is always preceded by a preamble which you do not find in any other Bills which go directly from the Table here to the Senate. But money Bills are presented by the Speaker, and here is the preamble which we find in* the beginning of every appropriation Act which is a money Bill :
Most Gracious Sovereign :
Whereas it appears from a message from His Excellency the Right Hon. Sir Gilbert John Elliott. Earl of Minto, Governor General of Canada, and the estimates accompanying the said message, that the sums hereinafter mentioned are required to defray certain expenses of the public service of Canada, not otherwise provided for, for the financial years ending respectively the 30th day of June. 1902, and the 30th day of June, 1903, and for other purposes connected with the public service :	may it
therefore please your Majesty

And so on. Here is the preamble which characterizes what is known in the restricted language of parliamentary law as a money Bill, to which no amendment can be offered by the Senate. But there are many Bills which are initiated here by the Crown and which ifche upper House has no power to introduce. We have in this question before us a grant or an appropriation of public money, but it is not a money Bill in the restricted sense to which I alluded, though it is on the border line between a money Bill and a Bill of a public character, it has always been allowed to the Senate-under such circumstances to offer an amendment; but it does not follow that because the Senate may offer such an amendment tile House of Commons are bound to accept it without inquiry or discussion. Perhaps it might be said that under such circumstances the Commons might exercise the right of refusing to accept the amendments of the Senate, not merely to reject an amendment, but to deny to the Senate the power to offer any amendment to this Bill. But that would be carrying the doctrine too far. We have innumerable precedents where legislation such as provided for in this Bill has been amended by the Senate. No longer ago than 1898 a Bill was introduced into this House : An Act further to amend the Act respecting the Judges of Provincial Courts, an Act which involved the expenditure of money, and it was reported from the Senate with several amendments iti which the Senate asked our concurrence. These amendments were considered by the House of Commons, some were accepted and others were rejected; at all events their

amendments were not deemed an invasion of the privileges of this House.
Did the clause of that Bill involve an expenditure of money directly connected with the revenue ?

I could not say at this moment, because 1 have not had time to look into it, but there were Bills of this character, and I desire to make it perfectly clear that the point taken by my hon. friend is not absolute. May lays the practice down just as I have stated it, that the House may or may not, just as they please, consider the amendment of the Senate but that the Senate are not going beyond their privileges in offering amendments to Bills of this nature. This is what May says :
If otherwise unobjectionable, the Commons usually accept amendments by the Lords, which, though not strictly regular, do not materially infringe the privileges of the Commons; and they justify their conduct by an entry inserted in the 'Journal,' under direction from the Speaker, explaining the motives of the agreement, stating, for instance, that the amendments are verbal- further the intention of the House-carry out the intention of the Commons-make the provisions of the Bill uniform and consistent-are rendered necessary by several Acts recently passed-or that the amendment does not alter or otherwise affect any valuation or assessment of taxation.
But, May goes further, and I call tlie attention of my hon. friend to this authority"
Even when amendments by the Lords are an infringement of privilege, it is not the invariable practice of the Commons to assert their claim regarding amendments made to Bills that they have sent to the Lords, which dealt with the relief of the poor, or with municipal, county and local rates and assessments:	more especially
when those amendments affected charges upon the people incidentally only, and 'were made for the purpose of giving effect to the legislative intentions of the Commons. The difficulty also of separating those amendments from other legislative provisions or amendments, to which there was no objection, has frequently prompted their acceptance by the Commons.
Even if there is an infringement of the authority of the Commons by the lords, the Commons have sometimes accepted the amendments because they thought they were in the right direction, properly amending the legislation which they had sent to the House of Lords for their consideration. The position I take upon this is that the Senate in this matter have not abused their privilege. The Bill that is under consideration is not one of those money Bills which it is beyond their power to amend. Theyr have not violated any principle and even if there has been an infringement of the privileges of the Commons it is a case in which the Commons should not insist upon their rights.

I think this is an important matter and while I always listen with approval to my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) who is always industrious and thorough in his remarks he will excise me, I think, when I point out that the test of this matter is to determine whether it is a money Bill and what is the object of the Bill. I understand the object of the Bill is to settle the classes which shall enjoy a pension. I therefore do not regard it as a money Bill and the Senate have simply said :	We do not wish lieutenant
governors to be placed among those classes. Is it a money7 Bill or Bill which settles the classes who shall enjoy a pension ?
It provides for a pension.	*

The Bill itself provides for a pension. The Senate amendments simply7 says among those who enjoy a pension we do not wish to include lieutenant governors. It is really an amendment relieving tlie treasury to the extent that lieutenant governors are removed from the classes of people who shall enjoy a pension.
The Senate have no right to do that.
That would not make it any more right.

This is a case that comes to my mind. Suppose we sent up a Bill increasing the number of judges in tlie Supreme Court to ten. It would clearly, in so far as the revenue would be concerned, be a charge upon tlie revenue to provide for the salaries of ten judges. Bill (No. 265) respecting the Revised Statutes of Canada-(the Minister of Justice)- read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 2.

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that our statutes of Canada are not creditable; the clauses of statutes dealing with the same subject are different in lang-guage in almost every instance. That is not right, because it puts a counsel or an individual who wants to understand a statute to the necessity of interpreting each line of every statute, whereas if we had statutes divided into classes, and the sections of statutes dealing with the same subject couched in exactly the same language, this would be avoided. There ought not to be a comma different. Any one who is familiar with the construction of statutes knows that it is one of the nicest occupations to which a man can giv'e his attention, requiring not only a clear comprehension of language, but also an appreciation of the niceties of grammatical construction and the construction of sentences. I may say that attention has been brought to this matter by Judge Wea-therby in Nova Scotia, a man of splendid intellect, although he is rather erratic ; he has one of the most perfectly analytical minds that you can meet with. It is a pleasure to hear him interpret a statute, I have been very often pained to hear him take one of our Dominion statutes and tear it all to pieces and express wonder if we have any law officer in Ottawa who knows anything about law or anything else. I must say that I concur in a great deal of what he says, and I believe we should attempt to do what they do in England, have every statute and every section of a statute dealing with the same subject couched in exactly the same language.

I am afraid that my hon. friend is giving too high praise to English statutes. I notice that the judges there speak quite sarcastically of the English statutes.
' Mr. GOURLEY. The late Lord Thring did a great deal to cure that. I am inclined to believe that there is more accuracy and nicety of expression in the English statutes than in our own, although the House will agree that I am not inclined to unduly praise the English.
The Americans are your friends.

They do not pretend to accuracy of language there. I would suggest to the Minister of Justice that in these acts of incorporation which we are constantly passing, clauses conferring certain powers should be kept exactly the same in every case and that no man drafting an Act should be permitted to alter the language to the extent of a comma. Therefore I think this is a very important section, that we should have good draughtsmen ; we might have a very good lawyer who might not be a good draughtsman, as they are different gifts.
Absolutely.

A man might be able to tear an Act to pieces but to have a Bill properly drafted requires the knack of using language to express an idea nicely. That is a gift, and if it does not appear in a statute it makes that statute hopeless of construction. I hope the Minister of Justice will impress on the commission the fact that the Acts of this parliament should be expressive of the very nicest intentions of parliament in the most apt English. I intend to assist the Minister of Justice as much as I can in having our statutes put in the fewest possible words. This habit of using many words is a loose, unscholarly habit. A man who is not a scholar is eternally using a lot of words when a few would be sufficient. If you make a long sentence in a statute, you only involve it. and you leave it doubtful how a court will interpret it. I saw a judge the other day take a section of a statute and re-write it to show the exact meaning of the language, and the meaning which the legislature evidently meant it to convey, and the two things were as different as night and day. The members of this House should be scholars enough to be able to express their meaning in the clearest and most concise language, so that no judge could have any doubt about it.
On section 12,
What does that clause mean ?

That is taken from a corresponding section of the Act respecting the Revised Statutes of Canada, which was passed in connection with the revision of 1886. If we were to distribute the Revised Statutes, as we now distribute the ordinary statutes, that would entail very large expenditure. The statutes are now distributed to the members of this parliament and the local legislatures and to all the magistrates.
When will they be distributed ?

There are 154 statutes for revision, of which 48 have

been revised. Each commissioner is given several statutes to revise, then they meet every three or four months and revise the work of each, and the whole is subject to the control of the chairman, the ex-chief justice of the Supreme Court, who is probably the most competent man in Canada. According to Todd the term ' Money Bill ' is very restricted. My hon. friend knows that a member of parliament has to go to a minister in order to get an appropriation for a wharf, and it would be an easier matter for him to introduce a resolution in the House. It was to prevent such an abuse that it has been decided that, although the granting of money is a special privilege of parliament, still it cannot be exercised except on the initiative of the Crown.

If it must have the consent of the Crown because it disposes of the public revenue, every Bill which disposes Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
of public revenues, and which must be introduced by a resolution and a declaration that it has the assent of the Crown, must be regarded as a money Bill.

Bill (No. 268) respecting the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada (The Minister

of Justice), was read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1-rank and salary of registrar.
What are you making Mr. Cameron's salary ?
It is to be $3,500 with annual increases of $100 up to a maximum of $4,000.
He is an excellent officer and ought to be well paid.

Whenever the salary of any lawyer attached to any court is up for consideration, you will always find some other lawyers to rise in this House and say something complimentary. What are the requirements of this position of registrar of the Supreme Court ? Why should we have an officer who is to be paid so large a sum ?

I have had considerable experience with that court, and may be in a position to say something in answer to the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Haggart). The registrar of the Supreme Court is not merely an officer of the court as that term is usually understood ; he is a judge. He is called upon, as registrar of the Supreme Court to sit in chambers, to hear and determine all applications of a rlhitine character-with reference to printing of cases or dispensing with printing, with reference to applications for costs, for leave to appeal, and so on. He sits almost every day.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Belcourt) allow me to ask him a question ? What is this officer's business ? What does he do outside of this ?

I am only explaining what the nature of his business is, and try-inig to show that those duties are more than the duties of an ordinary clerk of an ordinary court. The salaries of prothonotaries and registrars of courts throughout the land are perhaps not equal to the salary provided for, except in one or two instances. The registrar of a court, as a rule, has no judicial duties to perform ; he is simply a cleric of process, signs papers in processes of court, but does not adjudicate upon matters. But the registrar of the Exchequer Court is really one of the judges of the court, hearing and determining applications in chambers. It is true there is an appeal from his decision to a judge and from the judge to the court. The fact remains, however. that the registrar performs judicial duties every day. He is also the custodian of the library, has the responsibility of the books there and
We pay a librarian, whose salary I see is to be increased to a very handsome one.

But the registrar has charge of and responsibility for a very large and very valuable library, probably
the best legal library in Canada. Such a duty does not devolve upon the clerk of an ordinary court. I think this is the only court in the land which has a large library, the responsibility for which rests upon the registrar.
What has the librarian to do ?

He furnishes books and has charge of the routine of the library, but the responsibility for the care of the library rests upon the registrar. He has to make recommendations from time to time as to additions to the library. I think I am in the judgment of every member of this House when I say that the present registrar of the Supreme Court is a very deserving officer, and, I think, fully entitled to the remuneration provided under this Bill.

He may be a very deserving officer, but is it requisite for the administration of justice that such a deserving officer and a person of such ability should hold this position ? I do not say anything derogatory of the individual who occupies the office. I do not even know' him. After all that, he says, his duties are not judicial, they are principally ministerial- applications for orders and things of that kind, which do not require a judicial mind at all. These applications do not require an intellect of the order that is required for the Supreme Court. You may have for registrar a gentleman of greater intelligence and ability than are needed for a registrar, but that is no reason why you should pay him so high a salary. We could get a man to fulfil what I might call these mechanical duties for a less salary. I have noticed continually in this country when you establish a court, that first of all we have the judges, a short time afterwards there is a library established, then soon after, three or four messengers, then a librarian, then a couple of officers of court, and every session demands for an increase of salary. There is no other country on the face of the globe that is so encumbered with a superfluity of the administration of justice. No other race but the Anglo-Saxon race would submit to it. They are improving it over in Great Britain, but on this side it is getting worse every year.

I would like to ask the Minister of Justice if the Minister of Trade and Commerce was consulted in this matter, or the leader of the House. These gentlemen sit complacently by and see these increases voted for every man high and low. The salary has been increased all over. How the Minister of Trade and Commerce used to sympathize with the ratepayers when he was sitting on this side of the House. We were told that the poor ratepayers and the poor farmers were being bled white by the Conservative government. Now, this government is voting millions

upon millions, and every official in this country from Dan to Beersheba is, getting an increase of salary, and the hon. Minister of 'trade and Commerce is sitting there complacently, listening to the explanation given by the Deputy Minister of Justice about this official being a very judicial man and being responsible for the library. Now, how does he reconcile that with what he told the electors of what he was going to do after his friends got into power.
Keep your face straight.

Well, I can't keep it any straighter than it is. I am speaking with conscientious motives, and if hon. gentlemen can smile under the present circumstances, why they can smile upon going to the gallows. They have broken every pledge they gave to the electors in reference to economy, and how they can smile at hearing these things told them is more than I can understand. I heard tell of a man who was going to the gallows, and he met a man running that way and asked him what he was running for and when he told him : Well, he said, you need not be in a hurry, there will be no fun until I get there. But this is a serious matter. Here are broken pledges. I am not accusing the Minister of Justice of breaking his pledges, because he was not in the House then, but he is just as much responsible for it as those hon. gentlemen, because he has become one of them. He is endorsing them while they are breaking every promise they ever made to the people. I challenge the hon. gentleman to point out to me one pledge they gave to the electors when they were in opposition that they have carried out since they have been in power. The Postmaster General

Oh, spare me.
Mr. COCHRANE-used to tell us about the iniquities of the Conservative party, he used to tell us how humiliating it was for members of parliament to be sitting in the House with promises of office and emoluments in their pockets, and he even brought in a Bill condemning the practice. Is that hon. gentleman now carrying out the pledges that he made in opposition ? How many members of parliament have he and his friends appointed to office ? The Minister of Customs used to make the roof of this building tremble with his sonorous voice denouncing the extravagance of the Conservative party. Now he thinks it is all right. He thinks this gentleman is entitled to a large increase because he is responsible for the library, and because he has got a judicial mind. I don't care what kind of a mind he has got. We don't require a man with such a mind. A man with a very ordinary mind would be sufficient to do that work, and have plenty of time to lark around the country besides.

I always stand up for my hon. friend from East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) when he is condemning the government for breaking their pledges. His evident sincerity certainly convinces me, and I fancy it must convince bon. gentlemen opposite. But in the meantime we are discussing the salary of the registrar of the Supreme Court, and I desire to say that I think the policy of Canada has always been wrong in demeaning the public service of this country by paying insignificant salaries. The Supreme Court, if it is to be such a court as it ought to be and entitled to the respect of the people, must be a dignified tribunal, and everybody connected with it must be paid a sufficient salary to give dignity to the court. Every man in this country desires to see the Supreme Court possessed of a good library, with good officers to look after it, men competent by their legal intelligence to answer questions that may be asked them. When a man in a hurry goes into the library he wants to find a man there competent to give him assistance. The policy of paying everybody in the highest court in the country, salaries befitting the position, is one that I am sorry to say has not been followed in the past as it should be. These hon. gentlemen did not have these views when they were in opposition. We are setting them an example now of what an opposition should be in Canada,' and when you gentlemen get into our position, as you will in a short time, we hope-you will follow our good example. I know Mr. Cameron very well, he is a man of ability, he is a lawyer. He wrote a book some time ago, and it was so well written that it completely deceived me, because I thought X was reading the memoirs of an old member of parliament, but it turned out to be the mere creation of the imagination of our friend Mr. Cameron and a very bright little book it is. I go the full length of saying that that gentleman's salary as proposed here is not any too much for his abilities. X do not very often have the opportunity of finding myself in agreement with the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) but in this academic matter I am very happy to agree with him that Mr. Cameron is deserving of this additional salary. I want to say a word also in regard to Mr. Bligh, the librarian of the Supreme Court. I am bound to say that his salary is utterly insignificant and that he should not be required to live in Ottawa and maintain his family for the tu'penny ha'penny salary he is getting.
What is his salary ?
Do you call that a tu'penny ha'penny salary ?

If you had a good kennel of dogs you would require more money a year to keep them than that. If you want

any politics the whole thing is to be blamed upon the Liberal party in this country who sat here for eighteen years and kept down the remuneration of the members of this House. The remuneration of the members ought either to be nothing or it ought to be more. It is an honourable proposition to come and serve your country freely and I will go in for that if you like, but when you come to discuss the question of indemnity and put it at $1,500 it demeans every man in this House by making him a cheap man. When I was coming up from Nova Scotia a short time ago I met a bright, intelligent young man from Massachusetts, a Harvard graduate who is taking a post graduate course in economics for the purpose of fitting himself for public life in the United States. He found out that I was a member of the House of Commons and in the course of the conversation he asked me what the indemnity of a member of the House was. I avoided the question. I refused to tell him because if I had I am persuaded he would have thought that I was coming to a fifth-class country debating society instead of to the parliament of my country. Therefore I am bound to say that everything is insignificant and mean in this country in reference to the remuneration paid to public men. If there is to be an indemnity it should be higher than it is. How can one of those civil servants who perhaps receives a salary of $4,000 or $5,000 a year have any respect for a member of parliament who is given $1,500 to put into his pocket. We should either abolish the indemnity or fix it, at an amount which will be creditable to the people of this country. However, if we are going to treat ourselves-; meanly I do not want to treat anybody else meanly and therefore I support this increase to Mr. Cameron.

It is rather invidious to discuss individual cases, but this officer, like a great many others in connection with the administration of justice, is well deserving of greater recognition at the hands of parliament than he receives now. I cannot help reminding my right lion, friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) how things have changed. Of course we have a great deal more money nowadays owing to the features of the national policy that have remained, but the principle surely is not affected by the exuberance of the condition of things. When I was Minister of Justice it was pointed out, that, under a very old law that had been left on the statute-book, the exceedingly small salary of the chief justice of British Columbia would be diminished by about $900 a year and owing to many considerations and many strong reasons a Bill was introduced to prevent such a result, the general feeling being that the judiciary all over Canada wasl very much underpaid. A modest Bill came before the House to readjust salaries, so that the incoming chief 448
Justice of British Columbia on the death of Sir Matthew Begby would not find that he had $900 less than the very small salary of is predecessor and my right lion, friend divided this House by opposing that measure and opposing it vehemently on the principle, that, while he quite agreed that the judiciary were not well paid, it was an outrageous thing to bring forward the case of an individual and to deal with it. He was opposed to even preventing an injustice being done in this case until the government were prepared to take up boldly the whole problem and deal with the different courts of the Dominion fairly and on the same principle. Of course at that time my right lion, friend knows we could not do it. We had not enough money to go around. But, to-day, every one knows that things have changed. Here we are going to pass invidious legislation. It is not the ease of the present incumbent of the; office receiving less than his predecessor, but this is only one of several cases in which the administration have taken up individual claims. In this very case in British Columbia, and I do not like to refer to it as I practise at the Bar in that province and my words may be misunderstood, it was proposed to increase the salary of the judge of the Vice Admiralty Court and to appoint the chief justice as judge of the Vice Admiralty Court. That would have left, the chief justice with the same income as Sir Matthew Begby had and a very small one it was, something like $5,000 a year. Chief Justice McColl died and this House will be surprised to know that the present chief justice is receiving less than Chief Justice McColl or Sir Matthew Begby because Mr. Justice Martin was appointed to be judge of the Vice Admiralty Court. So, the reduction of the salary of the chief justice actually took place. I think this is the only-case in Canada since the beginning of this movement in favour of increasing salaries in which a reduction of salary has actually taken place. While I do not begrudge a high officer like the registrar of the Supreme Court of Canada receiving a salary somewhat adequate to the position, I do object to such cases as that which I have mentioned standing, on the statute-books of our country. In a short time under this Bill the registrar of tills high court will rank ns far as salary goes very nearly as high as the chief justice of one of the provinces of Canada. While I.do not object to what is proposed under the Bill, I say that the case that was proposed years ago was far stronger, and if I were disposed to follow that line of argument I would be obliged to oppose this act of justice. The case as it was then put by the right hon. gentleman in insisting upon a readjustment of the salaries of the judges generally was far stronger than the present argument in favour of dealing with individual cases. I am surprised at the course which the govern-



ment have taken because I would have expected, in view of the opinion prevailing generally throughout the country that our judges are poorly paid, that a' more comprehensive measure would have been introduced and that instead of dealing with this officer only many of these cases-and I dare say there are many more such cases as that which I have mentioned-would have received due consideration.
My hon. friend (Hon. Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper) unfortunately, has been away a good deal and he has not evidently been made aware of what has taken place in regard to the civil service.
I was dealing with the judiciary.

I am speaking of the civil service. There was an agreement on both sides of the House that the salaries of the civil service, ought to be increased, but the Civil Service Act is rather a complicated one and Mr. Cameron has been left out of the provisions of the Bill which was passed by this House some time ago. We thought it only fair that the Bill should be supplemented by this one so as to include Mr. Cameron in the benefits of the disposition which we have made of the matter.
With regard to the judiciary, I think that we will have to take up the subject at some time and to take it up sooner rather than jater, and to increase the salaries which are not sufficient at lore-sent. The question is not without difficulty. Here is the opinion of the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) that we are cursed with too many judges.
That may be ; too many judges too poorly paid.

I do not know that we could get on with fewer judges than we have. It may be said, in one sense, that we have too many governments in Canada, but that is the consequence of our system. On the whole, it is a good system. It has its inconveniences, but we have federal courts and we have provincial courts, and I do not think we have too many judges. We must necessarily have a large number of judges in proportion to the population, but if we consider that the population is scattered over a very large extent of territory in Canada, I think my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) will agree, on consideration, that it is impossible to have fewer judges than we have, although it may so happen that at some points there will be too many judges, at other points there may not be judges enough. That is a consequence of the condition of things that prevails at the present time, and which can be remedied only by the hand of time, when time shall have distributed population more

equally over Canadian territory than it is at the present moment. On the whole, there are not too many courts, but we have this unavoidable feature of our system, that at some points the judges have too much to do while at other points they have not enough to do, and the question is always brought up when these questions are under discussion. The man who is able to devise a plan by which the work will he more equally divided between the judges will have brought about a systeiu which the government will be only too glad to adopt.

It applies to the librarian and the assistant librarian of parliament also.

It applies in the same way as to the deputy head of a department under the Civil Service Act Amendment Act. If an officer had three years of service to liis credit when this Bill goes into effect he would commence at $3,800 and would then receive $100 for each year; if he had four years to his credit he would get $3,900, and If be had five years he would commence, as the hon. gentleman says, at $4,000. That is working exactly in the same way as in the case of the salaries of deputy heads of departments under the Civil Service Amendment Act.
How long would it take a deputy head, starting at $3,500 to reach the maximum ?
Five years.
Does the time of these officers count from the date of the passing of this Act or from a previous date ?

As I understand the Act, it applies from the passing of this Act except, that where an officer has been a few years in office, it applies from the time of his appointment. The gentleman in question has been in office for five years, in which case he would now receive $4,000 a year. A new appointee would commence at $3,500, and his salary would raise $100 a year.
It seemed to me that the Act was so worded as to show that it was intended to conceal its purpose from the general public.

It is drawn in the exact terms of the Civil Service Amendment Act as it applies to the deputy heads of departments, and it is intended to treat these gentlemen in exactly the same way as the deputy heads are treated.
What will be his salary next year under this Act?
The salary of the registrar of the Supreme Court under this will be $4,000 a year.

This is an increase of $800 at once. * I must protest against any such expenditure as that. Here is an officer of the Supreme Court, who has none of the qualifications of a judge, starting with a salary of $4,000 a year, nearly double the amount that a county court judge gets.
Some of them have other allowances.
Some of them have not.
I think all of them.

Not the juniors and some of the others. They get no allowances whatever and here is an officer of the court with a salary of $4,000 a year and a rise from last year of $800. There is no justification for such an increase.
Exactly the same as the deputy heads under the Civil Service Act amendment.

What justification is there for a man who receives an ample salary getting an increase at once of $800 a year ? This will give him $4,000 a year as registrar of the Supreme Court-a clerk. It is a monstrous salary.
A monstrous salary for the position ?

Yes, for the registrar of any court.
448J
I am afraid my hon. friend has not been here while the hon. member for Ottawa has been asking for an increase for the whole civil service.
There are many of us who represent other opinions than those of the civil service. Any man representing the city of Ottawa would advocate an increase for the civil service.

The feature which seems to me to be entirely unreasonable is the giving of an increase of $800 in one year. I could understand an official getting an increase of $50 or $100 a year until he reached the maximum ; but these last three cases together amount to an aggregate increase of $2,400 to three employees in one year.

The salary of the registrar of the Supreme Court originally fixed by statute was $2,000. Afterwards that was increased to $3,200. The object of the present amendment is to add $300 to that, making it $3,500. Then it goes up by annual increments of $100 until it reaches the maximum of $4,000.
He gets $4,000 immediately, because you give him credit for his back time.

His five years of service are taken into account, just as was done a moment ago in the case of the librarians. The hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) says it is absolutely unfair to pay the registrar of the Supreme Court such a salary as this. Why, the Master in Chambers at Osgoode Hail gets $4,000, though occupying a less important position. This gentleman sometimes sits as a judge, and there is an appeal from his judgment to the Supreme Court.
If he takes any responsibility upon himself, he consults the judges of the Supreme Court before venturing an opinion.
That is a matter entirely discretionary with him.
Would the hon. Minister of Justice answer this question : What is the immediate effect of this Bill upon his salary ? What does he get this year ?

At the present time he gets $3,200. By this Act he will be entitled to an increase of his salary up to $4,000. He will get $3,500 now and an annual increment of $100 a year. The Minister of Agriculture directs my attention to the fact that he gets the benefit of his accrued services to the extent of five years. At that rate he gets $4,000. My hon. friend must remember that the salary is not an extraordinary one, in view of the fact that the province of Ontario pays $4,000 a year and

that the prothonotaries of Montreal and Quebec get $4,000 a year.

But under this Bill it may be posible that this person will get $4,600 a year, because this Bill makes his salary $4,000 apart from $600 a year which he receives as editor and publisher of the Supreme Courts reports.

The payment to him as editor and publisher of the Supreme Court reports is not made by statute, but by Order in Council. I entertain no doubt that the statutory salary would supersede the salary paid to him by Order in Council. If the $600 is not voted each year in the appropriation Act, he does not get it ; but we will put a clause in the Bill to make that absolutely clear.

Even then it is too much. I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that it would be better to have all these amounts put in the annual Appropriation Act. It seems strange that a registrar and a deputy head of a department should have a statutory right to their salaries, as have no other persons in the civil service.
Progress reported.

Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK,
dependent weighmaster where the grain is handled. A great deal of this grain is taken out of the elevators at Owen Sound, Meaford, Midland, Collingwood and distributed to the millers. Toronto, Montreal, Halifax, St. John
Suppose the grain never reaches one of these points. If I buy a carload of grain shipped from Owen Sound it never reaches
It is weighed at Owen Sound.

revote substantially corresponds with the mileage previously voted. There may be a difference to the extent of three or four miles in one case, but not beyond that.

Has the work been actually commenced in every case of a revote, or is this just hanging out the sign ? Surely we should not vote subsidies year after year unless there has been some earnestness shown by the parties getting these subsidies in going on with the work. I would like to ask if work has actually been commenced in each case, and surveys and estimates of the cost made ?

I think in some cases the work has not actually commenced. But I do not think that should be a reason for refusing to subsidize a road. The work in many instances is slow,- the promoters having difficulty in getting the necessary capital. We have to be patient, and give them time. If the promoters have a reasonable hope of carrying on the work, we should not refuse the subsidy, if the enterprise on its merits deserves it.

Is there any limit, or is it the intention to vote and revote the subsidies for all time ? There ought to be some evidence of good faith on the part of the promoters. I am not now criticising the character of the scheme at all; but I think we should have some information as to the policy of the government in matters of that kind. I do not think the Minister of Finance would be prepared to say that this parliament should vote and revote these subsidies year after year as often as they lapse, unless something has occurred in the meantime.
What harm does it do to revote them ?

In the first place, this parliament should only vote subsidies to the most deserving cases, and they should be bona fide cases in which men propose to | go on with the work. Surely the hon. gentleman does not advocate our going on voting bonuses to parties who in many cases are endeavouring to sell them out. To vote and re vote these bonuses has a tendency to give these promoters opportunities of making money out of these schemes. I do not think it is standing in the way of any proper enterprise to say that no subsidy should be voted to a railway project unless it has life in it, or unless its promoters are prepared to go on with it. I can understand cases in which unforeseen circumstances might arise ; but I do not think the hon. gentleman should ask us to pass any one of these revotes without giving us reasons for the delay in going on with the work.

It is not merely a question between the promoters and parliament. Even where the promoters might not exercise due diligence, as some might think, the community is interested in
the railway ; and if one company has failed, perhaps others associated in the enterprise might make it a success. We must not forget that these enterprises are for the benefit of those portions of the country through which they run, and the people residing and owning property there ; and if the promoters do not make satisfactory progress, that is no reason for refusing to grant aid, not merely to the promoters, but to the people of the country through which the railway runs. I am sure my hon. friend would not want to do that.

No, I am too good-natured for that. The hon. gentleman has made the best possible argument in support of my contention, in saying that the people are chiefly interested. Why should persons get a charter for a railway, and get a subsidy voted, and then hold back the enterprise year after year instead of giving the service to the people ? The Minister of Finance should not ask this House to revote a single subsidy where there has been ample time to go on with the work, without giving some reason why it has not gone on.

I might point out further that a subsidy of $3,200 a mile will never tempt capitalists to build a railway unless there is good hope that the road when built will pay.
