I do not think I could give a better reason. Even though the company be not making much progress, if the enterprise is in itself meritorious, we are doing, right in giving the subsidy.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria. Is the charter Dominion or provincial 1
Provincial.

This is subsidized by the provincial government. I am not aware that the mind of the hon. gentleman from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) was at all disturbed with respect to similar votes in the first five or six resolutions, and we had no reason to think that it would be any more disturbed with respect to this or any other item for the province of New Brunswick than it was with respect to the items for Ontario. Now, this railway company is a recognized, institution. The demands of the district are certainly very strong. Of course, in the summer they can get along nicely with that great highway, the St. John river; but when the river is frozen over they have no communication with the outside world except with the old fashioned vehicles.

I am surprised that the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Em-merson) should have dealt in such small politics as to say that any lion, member in this House would make a distincton as between provinces in these matters. I certainly should not have thought of accusing the hon. gentleman ; but he himself has taken a good deal of trouble to make it plain to us that he is ready to deal in that style of politics. I hope that no other member in this House will be so small as to consider what province these votes are going to. If the scheme itself has merits, we need not inquire what particular province it is to benefit. Had I been in the House I would have raised the same question with regard to other subsidies that I ask in this case. I am disappointed in the information we have had, and I am afraid we shall have to insist upon better, whether the railway is one for Ontario. New Brunswick or any other province, for we have a right to information. A company that was voted a subsidy three or four years ago. not having earned that subsidy and desiring its renewal, would naturally be expected to place before the Minister of Finance a complete and detailed statement of the reasons for delay, the chances of going on, and the possibilities of carrying out the work in the future. If the prospects for the future were no better than they were when the subsidies were voted. I think the duty of the Minister of Finance would be to refuse a subsidy. Of course, it is a very ingenious argument to say that the people of the locality arejinxi-ons for this subsidy. But the people as a whole should be protected. There are persons so evil-minded as to say that these

things answer a good purpose in an election. I do not know whether any such idea ever occurred to the Minister of Finance-
Never.

Of course, the hon. gentleman is innocent of these things, hut he may suspect that some people have them in mind. Perhaps the hon. gentleman had better be frank and tell the House that that is the reason lie decided to give this sub-isdy, and that he did not ask for any other reason.

When the ministers come beiore the House to put their estimates through, they come with accurate information and attended by their deputies. They are able, in case of a public work, for instance, to tell us what the expenditure has been to date, how the work is proceeding and what expenditure will be required for its completion. But we are asked to revote railway subsidies Without any explanation of what has been done or what it is proposed to do. It is high time we ceased to vote these subsidies unless we have definite explanations concerning them. All this is an instance of the reckless way in which millions of public money are voted by this House. I have made a rough estimate, and I find that subsidies are being voted for 1,500 miles of road. No explanations are given to us, not even encouragement held out to the people in the localities affected that these roads will be built. There is either a lack of earnestness, or something held in view that we do not know about. Certainly, no minister ought to propose in this House a vote of public money without an explanation as to how that money is to be applied. And, if the money has been voted before and not spent, we want to know why it was not expended before and whether it will be expended now.
To the Shediac and Coast Railway Company for a line of railway from Shediac to Shemogue and towards Cape Tormentine, in Westmoreland county, not exceeding thirty-eight miles, in lieu of subsidy granted by chapter S of 1900, item 25 of section 2.
Mr. CLANCY When was that subsidy voted ?

This is in the riding of the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson). If you will permit me to ask a question without charging that the only reason why I ask it is that this railway is not in Ontario, I would request an explanation of this vote.

This is considered a strong company. They have spent a good deal of money in surveys, but, as is well known, there have been difficulties in the way of financing such enterprises during the last two or three years. The company are in earliest. This is a section of country
that certainly is in need of a railway. It is a fishing section, and perhaps one of the richest agricultural sections of eastern New Brunswick. It is quite largely populated. The people raise large quantities of potatoes which they ship to Bermuda. They have to cart them to Shediac, where they are taken by the Intercolonial Railway. This long haul by road is a very great inconvenience, which would be overcome if the people bad a railway. I do not know that it would be a very promising investment, but certainly tlie railway would be of great convenience to the people living along that shore.
To the Mabou and Gulf Railway Company, Limited, for a line of railway from Mabou Coal Mines to a point at or near Glendyer, thence to Orangedale on the Intercolonial Railway, not exceeding thirty-four miles, a revote of subsidy granted by chapter 4 of 1894, and in substitution of the twenty-five miles subsidized thereby from Orangedale to Broad Cove.

I would call attention to resolution 62, under which a subsidy is proposed for an additional four miles of this road. This railway is connected with a large coal-mining district in Mabou in the county of Inverness.
Has the work been commenced ?
I believe the company are now engaged in the construction of the road. It is a very substantial company, chiefly of Americans who are developing the coal mines at Mabou.
Does the hon. minister observe that this subsidy was granted in 1894 ?
Not to the present company. The present company have only recently taken hold of it, and they are pushing forward the work energetically.

I imagine that one of the difficulties was that the former company held the charter and the subsidy until they could get their terms for disposing of both to the company that took it up. No doubt there is something in that, but after all it is not an isolated state of things. The hon. gentleman will agree that there ought to be some reasonable prospects on tlie part of those asking for the subsidy that the work will pay. The Minister of Finance is unable at present to give us that assurance. This business of exploiting the country in that way with the money of the people is one which we should not encourage, and I doubt whether parliament is in any case bound to make a revote to a new company, because the original promoters are bound to be bene* fited to some extent.

This is a revote of the mileage of the road for that district, but it is not a revote to tlie same company. Whatever my hon. friend may

suspect in other cases, he w ould be wrong in this case, because I happen to know that the old company lias no connection with the new one. This is a new company and a different name ; I do not think they even received the old charter. I think the one died and the other has come up as an entirely new venture.
19. To the Nova Scotia Eastern Railway Company, Limited, lor a line of railway from New Glasgow to Cross Roads, Country Harbour, thence to the town of Guysborough, and thence to the strait of Canso; with a branch from Cross Roads, country Harbour, aforesaid, down the Country Harbour river to the deep waters thereof, not exceeding 116 miles ; in lieu of the subsidies of 40 and 80 miles granted by chapter 7 *of 1901, items 4 and 1, respectively, of section 2. ,	63. To the Nova Scotia Eastern Railway Com-
' pany, Limited, for a line of railway from Dartmouth through the Musquodoboit valley to a point at or near Melrose to connect there with the railway mentioned in item 19 of this section, not exceeding 120 miles.

The resolutions 19 and 03 should be read together.
These are two roads which are now being *consolidated into one company. The one starts from Dartmouth, on Halifax harbour, traverses the valley of the Musquodoboit river through the county of Halifax, thence into the county of Guysborough and, passing a point called Melrose, goes to Guysborough and Mulgrave. Then there is a crossroad which leaves the town of New Glasgow and crosses this other railway at Melrose and goes on to Country Harbour. This enterprise serves the counties of Halifax, Guysborough and Pictou and runs close to Antigonish, if it does not touch it. It covers a large portion [DOT]of the eastern section of Nova Scotia, which is at present without railway communication.
Is there any portion of this road built or being built ?

The surveys have all been made and the people are at work on it now. There is a subsidy granted by the Nova Scotia government and a contract made with this company. The company is composed largely of Canadians : Mr. Fitzpatrick, of New Glasgow ; Mr. Stratton, the Provincial Secretary of Ontario ; and Mr. McCormick, a member of this House. It is an excellent company. They have made all their financial arrangements and completed their surveys. The Nova Scotia government granted a subsidy of $5,000 a mile over the whole railway.
Is the hon. member for *Guysborough in the company himself ?
No, I am not.
Is the Sir. Stratton the hon. gentleman from Guysborough refers to the gentleman of the name who is mixed up with the Gamey affair ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The Hon. Sir. Stratton, Provincial Secretary of Ontario, is associated with these gentlemen that I have named.
At what point has construction commenced on this road ?

Between New Glasgow and Country Harbour.
For a line of railway from Debert 3tation on the Intercolonial Railway to Debert Coal Mine, not exceeding 4% miles, in lieu of the subsidy granted by chapter 8 of 1900, item 29 of section 2.
This is in the county of Colchester. It is a new coal mine which is being opened up now.

A short line like this should receive a larger subsidy. In Nova Scotia, unfortunately, the coal already discovered is north of the Cotoequid Mountains; this mine in the county of Colchester is south of the Cobequid Mountains, and if we could once discover a coal mine there it would give to the southern part of the province a great advantage in giving us cheaper coal. What is the use of giving a company that is struggling to open a coal mine a little subsidy of $3,200 a mile to build a railway ? You might as well send them down a pound of candy, If this parliament wants to command the respect of the people of Canada it ought to make a little vote like this at least $6,000. I supported a vote of $13,000 a mile for Mackenzie & Mann to *build railways in the territories, at least we are giving them a guarantee of $13,000 a mile, and I would take that in preference to this. Down in Nova Scotia we have not the commercial development to make railways pay. What is the good of a coal mine that is ten miles away from a railway ? I want to say that no railways in Canada should be more than eight miles apart, no man should be more than four miles away from a railway. If we who are members of parliament had to go four miles away to catch a train for Montreal we would think it a hardship. We want to have the trade brought to our doors. That is only a question of travel, but suppose one had sheep or cattle or other agricultural products to ship, and we had to go four males away to ship those products. Yet members stand up in this House in opposition to the building of railways ! If the members of this House want railways at their doors, what do you think of the case of a man in Nova Scotia, or in any other province, who has to go 20 miles to a railway ? The thing is preposterous. You oannot expect a great province like Nova Scotia to be developed unless you give it ample railway facilities. If $3,200 a mile is not enough, give $6,000 a mile ; and if $6,000 is not enough, make it $12,000 a mile. We want railway development, because, if we have railway development, we will have commercial development, and we will pay back tenfold every cent of money you hare given us, but we

want, in tlie first instance, the hand of assistance. This coal company have entered upon a large enterprise in a locality about which there is some doubt as to the financial outcome, and if we help this company we should grant aid to the extent of $6,000 or $8,000 a mile, and not the petty sum of $3,200.
If my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley) will read the first paragraph, he will see that these people can get $6,400 a mile.
Yes, if the cost exceeds $15,000 a mile. You tell me to spend $10 and then you will give me one dollar.
Would the company take $6,400 per mile rather than a guarantee of $13,000 per mile of their bonds ?

I think they would rather take the guarantee. In this case, as this vote is intended to develop a large coal interest in that part of the country, I think it should be an exceptional vote, and I think the vote should be raised to double the amount.
For a line of railway from a point on the Joggins Railway near River Hebert Railway bridge to the village of Minudie, not exceeding six miles, being a revote, and in substitution of subsidy granted by chapter 4 of 1894.

Is this the original
Joggins Railway ?
This is not the Joggins Railway. It is for a line from a point on the Joggins Railway.
Is this being voted to any company, or being voted generally ?
This is being voted generally for a line of railway.
And up to the present time no person has taken it up ?
Apparently not.
Is there any prospect of the road being built ?

Perhaps my hon. friend the Minister of Finance will allow me to answer the question as I am familiar with the circumstances of the case. I think that about the year 1885 a subsidy was voted for this same line of railway, but the coal development in Nova Scotia was not then in a flourishing condition. Within the last two or three years a number of lines have been opened up. The River Hebert mines are being operated by some Montreal capitalists known as the Minudie Coal Company, by the Strathcona Coal Company, and by seme American capitalists known as the Jubilee Coal Company. They are getting out a large quantity of coal, and the purpose of this railway is to give them an outlet on the water at Minudie.
Is there a charter for the road ?
Yes, a charter has been obtained for the road, and these companies are all in active operation, but are seriously handicapped by the fact that they have not proper communication with deep water.
This is to a point on the Joggins Railway.

No, from a point on the Joggins Railway to Minudie.
To the Middleton and Victoria Beach Railway Company, Limited, for a line of railway from Victoria Beach to Middleton, not exceeding forty-one miles, in lieu of subsidies granted by chapter 8 of 1900, section 2, item 28, and chapter 7 of 1901, section 2, item 21.
We want some explanation of this.

This road starts from Middleton, in the Annapolis valley, and follows the Annapolis river down the Granville shore to Victoria Beach, which was the objective point of the original designs for railway construction in western Nova Scotia. At present this railway is being amalgamated-I do not know whether legislative proceedings have been taken-with the Mackenzie & Mann system of railways in the western part of Nova Scotia. It was originally undertaken by another company, but I understand that it is to be consolidated with the Mackenzie & Mann system. It will run through some of the finest farminig land, I think I may say. in the world, because the Annapolis valley is the garden of the world.
Is this part of the road projected to Yarmouth ?

No, we will come to that later.
To the Halifax and South-western Railway Company for the following lines of railway:-
(a.) for a line of railway from a point at or near Halifax to a point on the Central Railway at or near Mahone hay, not exceeding sixty-eight miles.
(b.) for a line of railway from a point on the Central Railway at or near Bridgewater towards Barrington Passage, not exceeding 77 miles.
(c.) for a line of railway from a point at or near New Germany on the Central Railway to a point at or near Caledonia, not exceeding 22 miles.
(d.) for a line of railway from a point at or near Caledonia to Liverpool, not exceeding 29 miles.
The subsidies to the said lines of railway being granted in lieu of the subsidies granted by chapter 7 of 1899, items 17, 18, 35 and 36 of section 2, by chapter 8 of 1900, items 26 and 40 of section 2. and also chapter 7 of 1901, items 5 and 23 of section 2, respectively.
To the Halifax and South-western Railway Company for a line of railway to Barrington Passage, in addition to and in continuation of the 77 miles mentioned in items 23 (b) of this section, not exceeding 35 miles.

Subject to the addition of 35 miles, the vote for which you have just read, Mr. Chairman, these votes are a consolidation of a number of votes which have been given in past years for railway lines in the western section of Nova Scotia, westward of Halifax, running through the western part of Halifax county and the counties of Lunenburg, Queen's, Shelburne and Yarm'outh. These roads have been chartered in times past by various companies, and subsidies have been granted fron>
time to time to different companies. These various companies have not made very great progress. One of th'em built some part of one of these roads, but they were not able to carry it out. During the last year a consolidation of all these interests was effected by a company promoted by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann. They have made a contract with the government of Nova Scotia for the greater part of this enterprise on, the basis of a loan which the government of Nova Scotia are making to them on the credit of the road.
How much is the loan ?

Thirteen thousand per mile. Of course, they have proceeded on the assumption that they would get revotes of the Dominion subsidies. There are practically two lines, although there is a point at which they join. The main line will run from Halifax through the western part of that county, and through Lunenburg to Mahone bay. There it will form connection with the Central Railway of Nova Scotia, which is already owned by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann and their associates. It will use the Central Railway for a few miles, until it reaches Bridgewater. It then runs down the south shore of Nova Scotia to Barrington Passage, where it meets a road built from Yarmouth eastward. For the present this road is in different hands, but it is reasonable to expect that it will come into the possession of Messrs. Mackenzie & Maun. This vote, therefore, is to secure a road by the south shore of Nova Scotia from Halifax, passing through the western portion of that county, through Lunenburg, Queen's and Shelburne as far as Barrington, where it will meet a road already in existence running into Yarmouth. From Middleton, in the county of Annapolis, to Lunenburg the Central road has been in operation fcr a number of years. The second part of the new scheme leaves the Central road at New Germany, and runs to Caledonia. About 22 miles have been constructed, but not completed, under the charter known as the Hervey charter. That road has now been acquired by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, who are pushing it down to the town of Liverpool. This is a revote of various amounts for railways through these counties, with the addition of 35 miles necessary to complete the whole enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: How do they intend to get into Halifax ?

They have no terminal facilities at Halifax as yet, but I presume they will approach the government and try to make arrangements for using the government facilities; but there is no understanding on that point yet.
Has the province of Nova Scotia given any subsidy ?

They
have given a loan of $13,000 per mile to most of the line with a provision, I think, that in the event of the loan being repaid, the usual subsidy be deducted. For the present there is no subsidy, but if the enterprise is successful and the railway can repay the loan, then they may repay the loan less the subsidy.
Mr. IvAULBACH. Permit me to say, Mr. Chairman, that I am pleased that the government has fully realized how essential the completion of the work on this railway so long delayed, is to the people residing in the near vicinity of this road, running from New Germany to Caledonia.
Northern Queen's-part of the country represented by my hon. friend the acting minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Fielding)-has come into prominence as an agricultural and mining centre, the latter so far being only in its infancy. The same may be said of Northern Lunenburg, taking in Pleasant river, Ninevah, Hemp-ford, Ohio, and New Germany, places through which this road passes, abounding in farm, forest and mineral resources; interspersed with lakes and streams, presenting a perfect panorama, and unsurpassed in any part of Canada, and it is not confined I may say to this section alone, for after leaving New Germany-a railway centre-as well as a land of promise, and passing eastward we enter a still more beautiful country with rich and varied resources. I refer to Foster Settlement, New Burn, Woodstock and New Ross, admirably adapted for agriculture, with forests, lakes and streams and thickly settled by a progressive people but without the advantages of a railway, and in this connection I must here state, that I will never feel satisfied until I can see a road built from New Germany passing through this country to New Ross, and down the valley of the Gold river, connecting with the Halifax and South-western Railway at Chester Basin, now under construction, for the purpose of giving these places the same facilities as their neighbours. There was a railway subsidy granted east from New Germany some years ago but for some reason unknown to myself it lapsed, which was unfair to these people.
In connection with construction work between New Germany and Caledonia I desire to again bring to the notice of the acting Minister of Railways and Canals and the government, that there are (quite a number

of claims held by parties against the railway company for labour and material supplied on construction, and 1 would here ask what provision has been made for the liquidation or payment of these claims ? I contend the government have the right-nay they have the power, and they should exercise it-to see that provision is made for the payment of all such legitimate claims, and to see that they are deducted from the cash subsidies due by the government to the company, notwithstanding the company having sub-let the work of construction to others. In any case I hold the government should arrange for the payment of these bills.
The work of construction and the material supplied on the road represents the true value of the road, and the labourers and the party suppliers, as I view it, are really creditors in every sense of the term, and should have the first lien on the road for their bills, and anything short of this would be viewed by a reasonable mind as unjust.
We find the grocer or trader who supplied stores, and other commodities, to the labourers and sub-contractors during construction, remaining unpaid, as well as parties who furnished sleepers, mechanics who furnished cut stone, and numerous other commodities, remaining unpaid. I would ask, are they not to be recognized as creditors, and their claims paid before one dollar is paid over to the company, or the president of the road, by the government, in the way of subsidies ?
The law recognizes every mechanic and labourer employed in the construction' of a ship as having an equitable lien on the vessel until all bills are paid, and in default of payment they can distrain or replevin the ship at will, the customs refuse a register and prevent her sailing until every bona fide claim is actually paid, or as an equivalent, a voucher shown of the claim being settled.
I contend that if claims such as I have described hold good against a ship, the same is applicable to a railway; the two are analogous, and the parties claiming bills for work performed and material furnished to this railway company, their contractors or sub-contractors, come under the same category, are creditors in every sense of the term, and entitled to the payment of all claims.
It has always been the policy of the Ontario government to withhold all subsidies for railway construction until all wages of workmen, in fact, every employee and supplier of material on construction have been fully paid, and I sincerely hope the same policy will hold and be observed by the government as respects the road from New Germany to Caledonia.
The advantage in this case as respects the New Germany and Caledonia road is that the federal and provincial governments have the matter of subsidies entirely in their
own hands, in so far as the payment is concerned, and I here appeal most earnestly, on behalf of the creditors, that the government pay not a dollar to the company for construction, neither to the promoters nor contractors, nor any person else on this road, until a public notice is given by posters, and in all the county newspapers of Lunenburg and Queen's, asking that all bills unpaid be sent to an agent or adjuster, appointed by the government to receive such claims, and they to decide upon the merits or demerits of the same. The payments should be made by the government.
I may be told the government are dealing only with the present company, and have nothing to do with the original contractors. This would be unjust, as the road would really this day have no value had it not been for the hard labour bestowed by the operatives and the material and supplies, such as sleepers and cut stone, furnished by traders. Should these parties, as creditors, now be told that their claims cannot be recognized, when the government have it in their power to pay them 1 I would consider it unjust. I know of some poor farmers and labourers who have had to sacrifice the little they possessed, and their families suffer, in consequence of the delay in payment of bills. I sincerely hope the government will realize the importance of this situation as respects these people, and see that the bills are paid after the manner I suggest.

We have been so long in Ottawa this session that some of us may be pardoned for being a little rusty on what is going on in our provinces. I am glad to say to my hon. friend (hat what he suggests has actually been done and that arrangements are being perfected at the present moment to carry it into effect. There is a full understanding between the Nova Scotia government and myself that the governments at Ottawa and Halifax will have to co-operate in the construction of these roads and that we shall jointly see that whoever undertakes to carry out the new enterprise, will have to provide for the paymeut of the honest claims of the workmen under the old contractors. I am glad to be able to assure the hon. gentleman that in carrying out this arrangement a commissioner was appointed by the local government some time ago. He is at this moment holding investigations in order to obtain correct statements of the amounts of money due, and I am satisfied that in every case in which a claim can be substantiated to the satisfaction of the commissioner, the money will be paid.
I am glad to hear the statement of the hon. acting minister. If he had only given me an inkling that such was taking place, he would have saved me the necessity of occupying the time of the House.
What amount of construction has been done on this southwestern Railway ?

The portion of the road from New Germany, in the county represented by my hon. friend, down to Caledonia was graded and the bridges built, but the rails were not laid. The new company is now laying the rails. The portion from Halifax towards Mahone Bay has been under construction, and considerable progress in that heavy section has been made. Workmen are now employed working westward from Bridgewater in the county of Lunenburg and on other sections. There is now more evidence of good faith in pushing on the work than has ever been shown before, to the great satisfaction of the people along the line ?

I am pleased to hear the statement made by the acting minister. May I ask him if they have fully settled on the location of that portion of the road near Fort Medway, whether it is to go east or west of Mill Village ?

We have not yet been called upon to approve officially of any of the plans of this road, because until the subsidy is granted, we are not in a position to demand any plans from the new company for approval, and, we have not taken any formal action in regard to the location of the road. My impression, however, is that the line that commends itself to the people goes below Mill Village towards Port Medway.

I think that would be a mistake, because there is a valuable industry in the shape of a pulp mill two miles above Mill Village, which would be a source of traffic to this road which would not be the case if it went below that point.

That matter I know has been engaging the attention of the engineers. All questions relating to location of roads are full of difficulties of that character. I think there is no finality in the location ; but the engineers have rather come to the conclusion that a line below Mill Village would be more in the general interest than one above. I am aware of tlie pulp mill industry to which my hon. friend refers, and will endeavour in some way to see that it gets proper accommodation.
Has this road been located towards Barrington ?
I do not think there is any difference of opinion about the location of the Barrington end.
Do I understand that a connection will be made with the pulp mill ?

That remains to be seen. We may be able to do Mr. KAULBACH.
something in the way of providing communication by means of the river.
Have contracts yet been entered into with the different companies 1

Yes, some contracts were entered into and some construction took place ; but these contracts have all expired, and the subsidies lapsed. Therefore they have to be revoted. There has been no payment of subsidies to this company for this purpose.
Has there beeu any payment to other companies for this portion of the road ?

No, none whatever. They never got to the point of earning the subsidy.
To the Inverness Railway and Coal Company, formerly the Inverness and Richmond Railway Company, Limited, for eight miles of railway between Point Tupper and Broad Cove; and for a line of railway not exceeding thirty-seven miles from Cheticamp to a point on the line already built between Broad Cove and Point Tupper, being a revote and in substitution of the subsidy granted by chapter 4 of 1897.
Hon.' Mr. HAGGART. What is the change ?

This is ft road known as the Inverness and Richmond road, now called the Inverness Railway and Coal Company, running from Port Hastings on the Strait of Canso up to Broad Cove. A portion of the road is built, up to that point, and this revote is for the portion from the terminus up to Cheticamp. It also provides a rearrangement of the mileage, without any addition, which will afford a shipping point on the Strait of Canso.

I believe this road was originally surveyed from Broad Cove to a place called Chimney Corner and from there to Cheticamp. Is it proposed to extend the same railway from Broad Cove to Chimney Corner and thence to Cheticamp, or is it proposed to build it by way of Mar-garee Forks ?

That is a question of location which I am not able to answer.
For a line of railway from a point at O'- near Wolfville on the Dominion Atlantic Railway to the government pier on the basin of Minas, not exceeding one mile, in lieu of the subsidy granted by chapter 7 of 1901, section 2, item 19.
This is an extension from the Dominion Atlantic Railway down to the public wharf at Wolf-ville. There is a corresponding vote for the other side of the bay, which will be reached later on.
For wliat purpose is this to lie constructed down to the wharf ?

There is a public wharf at Wolfville. Steamers cross

the bay from Parrsborough to Wolfville, and it is proposed to make an extension on one side and on the other so that passengers may be brought direct to the wharf instead of having to travel some distance.
Is this a public wharf ?

Yes, it
is a government pier.
To the Nicola, Kamloops and Similkameen Coal and Railway Company for a line of railway from a point at or near Spence's Bridge on the Canadian Pacific Railway to Nicola lake, not exceeding forty-five miles, being a revote of subsidies granted by chapter 5 of 1892 and chapter 4 of 1894.
Why is this not proceeded with ?

The company now applying for this subsidy is not the original company. It has got a charter, and I understand it will get a provincial subsidy. I am informed that it is going right ahead. It goes through a good district, and will open up the Nicola valley which at present has no railway communications, also the coal deposits at the foot ofNicola lake.
Did the original company dispose of its charter to the other ?
No, the new company applied and procured a new charter and a Dominion charter.
What has become of the old company ?
It is defunct.
Does the company which proposes to build this railway own the coal mine ?
I am not positive, but I believe it does.
Did not the original charter run from near Kamloops to Nicola valley ?
This is to run right up to Kamloops as well. It goes from Spence's bridge to Nicola, and will go eventually to Kamloops.
The vote does not say anything about running to Kamloops. I think the old charter ran from Kamloops.
So does this, but the vote is only for forty-five miles of that road.
I do not wish to be understood as objecting to a coal company getting a subsidy. I do not know any good reason why a coal company should not have some assistance in building a railway.

The grant was originally given the Nicola Valley Railway Company, which failed to carry out its undertaking, and the petitions for this com-1 449
pany asked that it be given the powers conferred by the charter to the old company, and that the subsidy granted to the old company should be continued to it. This is giving to a new company a grant which was given to a former company.
For a line of railway from Winnipeg Beach or Teulon to a point on Icelandic river by way of Gimli, not exceeding thirty-five miles, in lieu of subsidy granted by chapter 7 of 1901, section 2, item 26.

The only reason for delay in the construction of this road, 1 may tell the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), has been the scarcity of labour, it has been absolutely impossible for the railway company to get labour. There is no objection to this grant.

A year or two ago, when the charter was being considered, the Canadian Pacific Railway were obliged to construct up to Winnipeg beach, a few miles north of Selkirk. Yes.

We have heard from an hon. member, who is a director of that



company, that lie entirely objects to anything of this kind. I thought then that he was expressinig the opinion of the company.

No, but they have applied for several others.
This session ?

Yes. This application came from the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), who thought there was a misunderstanding with regard to the previous vote. I do not think I have any application from the Canadian Pacific Railway for it.
This is a subsidy forced upon the railway company without any application at all.
They are uot obliged to take it.

I am not sure whether the Canadian Northern has a charter thews or not.

Mr. HUGHE'S (Victoria). There is no charter covering the railway along the lake shore to Gimli. There is a charter extending up the middle of the tract of land lying between Lake Manitoba and Lake Winni-pegosis on the west and Lake Manitoba on the east.

I do not know about that. .

This is an extraordinary thing. When the granting of these subsidies was first begun, one of the principles laid down was that a subsidy should be given only when a company had satisfied the government that they were possessed, not only of the desire, but of the financial ability to build the road if they were aided, but that they were unable to build it without aid. But the minister tells us that no company has applied for this subsidy. And he tells us that the company holding the charter is the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is well able to build, and they have not asked for a dollar. He says that the hon. member for the riding has asked the government to assist in building the railway, and he is handing it over. I presume, as a free gift to the Canadian Pacific Railway. In many other parts of the country

where companies desire to build roads, they have not been able to get the assistance of the government. But in this case we are so lavish with our money that we are ready to give it to a company whether they ask for it or not.

I did not know that we were here legislating for any particular corporation. There are 5,000 people in that section who have been settled there for twenty-five years on the promise made in this parliament that they should have a railway to enable them to ship their wood, and so clear their land. That promise has never been carried out. On behalf of these people I asked that a sum of money should be offered to any company that would give the desired railway accommodation. I am not speaking for the Canadian Northern Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway, or any other corporation.

That was not the principle upon which these subsidies were begun. As I say, the object of a subsidy was to assist a weak corporation to build a railway that it could 'build with a subsidy, but it could not build without a subsidy. It is uot contended that this road is to be built by a weak corporation requiring assistance. The corporation that is expected to build it is known to be strong. We have not even an application from this company for the subsidy.

We have not any offer from the company to build it. It is not certain, I suppose, that they will build the road for the subsidy, but it seems reasonably certain that thej will not build it without it. The fact that a company has not applied for a subsidy does not prove that one ought not to be offered. My hod. friend from North Grey (Mr. Sproule) has confused the conditions. The principle is that before you enter into o' contract with a company to build a road and receive the subsidy, you should have reasonable assurance that they are acting in good faith and have the resources to build the road. But it has not been said before that you shall not grant a subsidy until some company has shown itself able and willing to earn it-. Again and again subsidies have been voted in order to try to find a company to build a road.

I say that the principle when we commenced the granting of railway subsidies was laid down in this House, and it was that when a company was prepared to build a road, but needed assistance, that assistance could be given.
That was as respects the making of the contract, but not as to the granting of the subsidy.

What is the general understanding under which subsidies like this are granted ? Does the first company com-

lng and showing evidence of good faith and ability to build the road receive the bonus ? Or, as between companies, does the government make a choice 1

The government must be trusted wiith discretion, inasmuch as the object is to get the road built. We hold out the subsidy hoping that it will induce somebody to build the road. But the government must have discretion in selecting the company. In this case we do not expect to be obliged to select from half a dozen companies all ready to build the road. I fancy this road will be built by the Canadian Pacific Railway and nobody else.

I think it oportune at this point to offer a few remarks on the policy of subsidizing railways in the older provinces of Canada. We have just gone through a list of railways which are applying for renewals of subsidies, which I presume, in many cases, have lapsed, covering mileage of some 1,500 miles, aggregating in cost something like $6,000,000. We now come to the consideration of subsidies for new lines of railways, making a total mileage of some 4,000 miles, and aggregating in cost to this country in subsidies from $16,000,000 to $20,000,000. It is not necessary to make any remarks on the large amount that is here involved, but we may notice that this is altogether outside and independent of the huge scheme we are facing of building a transcontinental railway. In face of this, I think it is time that we should call a halt and consider whether it is in the best interests of this country that the policy which has been pursued in the past should be continued. Occasionally when we ask the question why we should continue the policy of subsidizing railways in the older provinces, we are sometimes told in reply : Well that has been the policy in the past ; it has been in vogue for a great number of years, and we suppose it will have to go on. If there was ever a time when we should call a halt, in order to give this question a full, and further consideration before we go further, this is the time. It is questionable whether it is good policy to build a railway anywhere that cannot be built without a government subsidy. It may be a fair proposition that any railway which requires a government subsidy in order that it may be built is not required by the business of the country, or in the interests of the country, and probably would not be a paying enterprise. At this time capital Is seeking investment in any enterprise that will pay reasonably well in this country, and where there is really business to be done and a commercial need for the railway, there will be no need to go asking the various governments, federal, provincial and municipal, for subsidies to build railways. Any scheme of that kind that has a fair proposition to place before the capitalists of this country, is one which if brought under the consideration of men capable of looking into it, will not lack necessary capital for its construction. It may be argued that railways in the older provinces cannot be built without government subsidies ; I thinik it is a question whether they should be built at all or not. I know that it is said that this is the old policy. It does not follow that because it is a policy that has obtained in the past that with the changed conditions of the country, with the growth and development of the country it should still continue. It was perhaps necessary to build railways when the country was new, in order to open up the country, and it may be that in opening up new territories and new sections of this country, the policy of subsidizing may still be a wise policy, but in the older provinces, which are already supplied with the necessary transportation facilities, there is no call for further building of railways ; or if they are built, they should be built on such a sound business basis as would invite capital of its own accord to seek investment in them. It is not a sufficient defence to say that for many years we have subsidized railways. The changing conditions in this country remind us of a line of Lowell's that ' new occasions teach new duties,' and we might fairly consider whether it is not a proper time to depart from the old policy which has obtained in the past. The enormous amount involved in the subsidies we are asked to vote on this occasion, will only be added to from year after year ; a new batch will come up next year. The business of railway promoting has become a distinct profession, and men enter upon it, not for the benefit of the country, and not even in the Interests of capitalists, but as charter mongers, or promoters of railways in order that they may pull out of any scheme all they are able to get and leave the scheme to sink or float. We have had some notable examples of that in this country ; railways have been exploited by the promoters, who secured subsidies from the federal, provincial and municipal governments, pulled all the money they could out of them, and then allowed the railways to become bankrupt enterprises, not needed by the country, and with not sufficient business tributary to them to make them paying enterprises. In this connection, respecting railways to which subsidies have been granted and those to which subsidies will be granted in the future, I think it well to call the attention of the government to the fact that the interests of the workingmen, the men who put their labour, time and money into schemes of this kinid, should be protected in every way. We have had examples during this session of parliament in which men have supplied materials, &c., for the building of railways and in one or two instances have been left without pay, while the men who exploited the railways made all they could out of them and went away, you might say, with the government subsidies in their pockets. I think it would be a good policy for the government to call a halt and grant no more subsidies to railways, at least in the older provinces, until they have had

fuller and freer consideration, by a full parliament during the next session. A large number of the members have now gone to their homes, and the parliamentary representation of the country is at present very much depleted. A subject of the importance of tins one should not be dealt with at this late period of the session, but should have a full and fair consideration. These estimates ought to be brought down for the opinion of the House earlier in the session. It is not fair to parliament to ask them to consider the expenditure of such enormous sums of money in the dying hours of the session, in order that they may be rushed through without that full discussion which all subjects of this kind should receive. I believe that the good common sense of this country is largely opposed to subsidy granting. I know that in the section which I represent. among the farmers, public opinion is opposed to the granting of subsidies even for railways that may be constructed through the country in which they are living, and I speak as representing them. The burdens of this country ought to be lightened, and not so enormously increased as they are being. It is a question whether the best interests of the country are considered or the interests of the government. It is government patronage which requires these enormous subsidies more than the requirements of the country. These railways are, perhaps, being exploited more for that purpose than for the benefit they will be to the country at large.
While I am on this subject I might refer for a moment to the question of giving charters to railways. We have now had a railway commission appointed which we may presume will be of a non-political character. It would be but fair that every company seeking a charter to build a railway should have their project submitted to that railway commission, and thoroughly examined by them before parliament meets, in order to see whether such a railway would be in the interests of the country, whether it was demanded by the requirements of the country, and whether there would be business tributary to it sufficient to make it pay. We might then have good, solid legislation along this line, and not have railway enterprises such as have been brought before this House during this and the last session. I do not intend to occupy the House any longer, but I throw out these few suggestions in the interest of my own constituency, and I believe that in doing so, I represent largely the good common sense of this country.

This afternoon we somewhat hurriedly passed some thirty resolutions granting subsidies to railways, all of which, however, are revotes, renewing grants which had been made in former years, perhaps chiefly under the direction of the present government, but some of

them extending back beyond their advent to power. Possibly the same exception could not be taken to the renewal of subsidies that can be taken to new subsidies. No doubt in many cases men have entered into large financial obligations under promises from the government of the day that they would be aided- in the enterprises in which they had interested themselves, and consequently it might seem unfair for the government to refuse now to carry out in good faith what was promised to railway incorporators in days gone by, and on which they proceeded to invest their own money and the money of the shareholders they had secured throughout the country. Therefore, it may fairly be argued that the passing of these revotes is justifiable, and could not well be refused by the House. But when we come to the new subsidies, I think we can look at the matter in a very different light. It has been well said by the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) that it is time that we called a halt in the granting of railway subsidies. Many of these railways which We are about to deal with pass through well settled sections of the country, and therefore ought to be selfsustaining. I fail to see that the country at large is called upon to supplement what the promoters of these railways may be able themselves to put into the enterprises in order to make them paying speculations. Some of them I have no doubt have merit.
I do not for a moment say that we should in every instance refuse a subsidy to a railway. I think there are meritorious cases- roads which may be strictly called colonization roads, going into and opening up new sections of country. But to my mind the great bulk of them are roads which have no claims, and for which no subsidy should be granted by the government. It has now come to this, that you cannot build a mile of railway in this country' without coming to the government for assistance. In this list of subsidies which we are to deal with to-night, we have railways down to one mile in length, two and a half miles, three miles, four miles. Surely it is not necessary for the promoters of these schemes to come to the government for assistance. These short lines of railway do not lead into new districts; they cannot be classed as colonization roads. One of them is referred to as a road leading to a wharf. Surely it is not necessary for the government of this country to be called upon to use the public money to assist enterprises of that kind. Therefore, whilst there may be meritorious cases to which aid may be granted, I think the great bulk of these cases which we are about to deal with should not receive aid. 1 think the principle of subsidizing railways should not be continued to the same extent as in the past. I think the time has arrived in this country when most railways can be constructed and made to pay without the intervention of the government. I therefore
14349 [DOT]

desire to place on record my protest against tlie passing of these resolutions. I do not suppose for moment that will prevail. The government have apparently adopted this policy, and have gone very far. afield in widening it. It seems to me that they might have narrowed it down to cases of real merit. In saying this, I lrnow I am voicing the sentiments of my constituents. The feeling is very strong, not only in the county I represent, but I believe throughout western Ontario. Some may say that it is a rather selfish view and that western Ontario, having been well provided with railways, should not complain if other sections of the country are aided in the same way. I do not say that every case is lacking in merit; but I think that the government should exercise a great deal more judgment in the promises they are making to the promoters of railways, and that the number should be very much limited. I hope and trust that the government will take this view of the matter, and will consider the sentiments of the people of this country. If they do that, I am quite sure that a good many of these resolutions which we have before us to-night will not receive the endorsation of the committee.

The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) has in a general way protested against the granting of railway subsidies for the older parts of the country-I suppose having in mind particularly the older parts of Ontario. I hold in my hand a petition from a number of the electors of the county of Grey asking for the construction of a railway through that county. The hon. member for Haltou (Mr. Henderson) also protests against the granting of subsidies. These two gentlemen have the distinguished honour of representing constituencies which have been eminently served by railways, and those railways have received pretty liberal public aid. I am not aware that these gentlemen ever recorded their opposition to the construction of any railways projected through or calculated to assist their particular constituencies; but their constituents having got all they think they can profitably use, their representatives arise in this House and protest against other constituencies receiving as equitable a measure of treatment. My hon. friend from Halton probably thinks he is discharging his full duty by uttering a general protest against these subsidies. May I be permitted to point out to him a much more effective way of recording his objection ? If he is sincere, and I am sure he is, let him at the right time, before these subsidies are granted, arise in his place and point out by a distinct motion which subsidies in this list he objects to, and let him challenge the vote of this House, and place upon record by -yeas and nays the views of those who are either against or for these
subsidies. We then will know where we stand. There is scarcely a subsidy we have passed which has not been supported mord or less by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I venture to say that of those which are to come we will see the same liberal action on the part of members of the opposition. Until they by their votes challenge a particular subsidy, they cannot escape responsibility by entering a general protest against all subsidies. There is only one way in which my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) can put himself properly on record, and I now await with great interest to see whether he will take that proceeding- there is only one way in which he and his friends can put themselves on record and that is by recording their votes.

I am certainly grateful to the hon. Postmaster General for the fatherly advice he has given me-I might almost call it a lecture. But after an experience of fifteen sessions in this House, I am inclined to doubt that I require the special counsel which the hon. gentleman has offered. I have my own opinion on the question. I am quite willing to name the resolutions I object to and which I consider have no merit, and I will undertake to move a resolution, if the hon. gentleman will second and support it. That is the position I take.
A very safe position.

If the hon. gentleman will support my resolution, I will be happy to vote with him. I fear, however, that I shall be obliged to limit very materially the number of resolutions condemning these subsidies, if I desire to get the hon. gentleman's support. With regard to the mode of entering my protest, I know of no stronger way in which a member of this House can declare himself than by making a speech. It is an old saying that an hon. member can very easily explain away a vote, but he cannot explain away a speech. I think the Postmaster General will agree with me on that point and perhaps regret having made some of the speeches he did in this House, particularly not later than Saturday last, which he will have a great deal more difficulty in explaining away than if he had given a vote. I consider that I have given the strongest protest I can against this wholesale granting of subsidies, even though I may not have the privilege of voting for a resolution condemning it. The hon. gentleman knows1 that all the resolutions I could move here would be voted down by himself and his friends, and it would be useless for me to propose resolutions which would: not have the slightest chance of being accepted by the majority of this House.

The hon. gentleman, for once in his life, manifests a desire to become an humble follower

of the Postmaster General. I was not aware until this moment that he was ever prepared to take his views on public matters from any one on this side. He now says he is prepared to propose a motion to strike out all of these* subsidies, if I will second it. But I am not of his opinion. I am in favour of these subsidies and am prepared by my vote to support them. If my hon. friend is opposed to them, let him make his motion. He does not require to seek me for a seconder. He has his friends, let him see if he can get a corporal's guard of his own people to support him. He would like to go before the people and point out that he had made a protest against these subsidies, but he dare not call for a vote on any of them. He asks what is the use of proposing a motion which will be voted down. Since when did the hon. gentleman become so modest ? We have had vote after vote during these last seven months, called for by hon. gentlemen opposite, although they knew perfectly well that their propositions would be defeated. They regarded the taking of the yeas and nays as the proper way to place on record their views for or against any policy. How comes it now that my hon. friend changes his views and tactics ? I tell him and every member of the opposition that each one of them is responsible for every one of these subsidy votes unless he challenges a division. Let each man stand up and record his vote for or against. They cannot escape responsibility under cover of a general disapproval. They cannot escape responsibility to their own constituents by simply giving utterance to an idle protest. Let them place themselves on record. Let them come out like men. Fancy my hon. friend apologizing to the people of Halton for - not presenting a motion because the Postmaster General would not second it ! Would he not be asked whether he was sent to parliament to do what the Postmaster General approved ? He would be told that he was elected to oppose the Postmaster General. Yet to-night, under cover of a plea of that kind, he seeks to escape the responsibility which devolves upon him, as upon every other individual member of this House. I repeat that until he challenges by his vote any subsidy submitted to this House, he will be held responsible for having granted it.

The hon. gentleman has suggested that I wished to take him as my leader. I desire to disclaim any impeachment of that kind. What I did say was that I should become the leader of the Postmaster General, and I hope that before this debate closes I may find in him an humble follower.
Try me.
I repeat again that the protest I have made is the strongest I can possibly make. The Postmaster General

has instanced cases in which we on this side have challenged the policy of the government by moving resolutions. That I consider to be a very good plan, because it does not require every member to stand up in his place and enter a protest against the government policy when all of one mind, that can be done much more quickly by voting on the question. I do not know what is the policy of hon. gentlemen on this side on the question of railway subsidies. I do not know if they have any general policy, nor do I know whether hon. gentlemen opposite have such a policy. Perhaps there is not on that side behind the Postmaster General a united opinion. If he would test his own followers, he would find hon. gentlemen behind him who would much rather that we on this side did not move resolutions condemning these railway subsidies. If we did, some of his followers would be compelled to give a vote which they would much prefer not giving at this time. I desire to say nothing further. I desired merely to give expression to the sentiments of my constituents. My constituents know my sentiments and I know theirs, and so far as I am able, both by voice and by vote, if a vote should be taken, I am prepared without hesitation to put myself on record in favour of what I believe to be the sentiments of the people I represent.
As one of the corporal's guard, to which the hon. the Postmaster General alluded in his somewhat magniloquent manner, also I am prepared to make a general protest.
Hear, hear.

And I base that general protest upon the minute of council passed by these hon. gentlemen themselves appointing a responsible commission to investigate and pass upon the great transportation questions of this country. We should not touch the question of bonusing a single mile of new railway that should come within the purview of that commission until that commission has reported. And, as to any railways that do not come within the purview of that commission we have no right to deal with them at all. Our business here is to legislate with regard to matters for the general benefit of Canada, and local matters we should leave to local authority. Instead of that, we find ourselves called upon to deal with a variety of schemes about which even the government themselves know nothing. They are asked questions as to when charters were granted, why granted, to whom granted, and the hon. gentleman in charge of this measure knew nothing at all about these matters. And I do not think that the Postmaster General (Hon Sir William Mu-lock), with all due respect to him, knew any more. The government, so far as railway matters are concerned, is going merely

at haphazard. I may be mistaken, and they may know more than they appear to know; but I do not believe that the government really know anything about the schemes they have placed before us. We have heard to-day of one railway that was projected in the province of New Brunswick on one sidle of a river. It turned out that there was another railway a short distance away on the other side of the river. And the members of the government did not know how many miles these railways would be apart and did not know where the new railway was going.
I take the government to task upon their dealing with these questions after the appointment of a transportation commission. They have talked a great deal about that commission. Why should not all these questions be placed before them for consideration ? But the course we are now taking is that we appoint respectable gentlemen as a commission and then give them nothing to do. During to-day's sitting, before six o'clock, we had passed, I believe $6,000,000 of railway subsidies; and we are asked to pass now somewhere in the neighbourhood of $7,000,000 more. This government have become so accustomed to dealing in large figures that $13,000,000 is a mere bagatelle to them. But I am sure that the country Is taking a very different view of it. And if the government wish to make the im-presssion they desire to make, they should be prepared, when proposing to give $3,200 a mile for a certain length of railway, to give full information as to what that money Is being granted for and why the road should be built. Without such information, we do not know but that instead of subsidizing a railway we are subsidizing a constituency. We know very well that most of the votes this morning were revotes, some of them eight and' ten years old. Do you mean to tell me that you are subsidizing railways in such cases as these ? I make the general statement, as my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) made it. that in many cases these are subsidies to constituencies and not to railways. These railways were subsidized years ago and never built, yet these subsidies are renewed. And the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) endeavoured to terrorize members into voting for these subsidies. ' Challenge the vote,' he said. What does that mean ? It means that members should place the government in a position to say : These miserable fellows in opposition are opposing a vote of $3,200 a mile for a railway to run through this constituency; they are opposing the spending of that money in the constituency; but the government is quite willing that that money should be spent : Glorify the government! Why, it is mere child's play to deal with him in this matter, because we know his style of argument. Usually he is strong; but this evening he is remarkably weak. I think he was not himself at all in arguing this railway question.
Now, the government are face to face with another difficulty, a difficulty which they must feel. How are government debentures going in the financial market at the present day. Are governments, even endorsers of railway bonds, able to raise all the money they want ? And great railway systems, when they want to raise money, instead of paying 3 per cent, are they not obliged to go to New York and Great Britain and pay 54 per cent ? And this country is going to spend $100,000,000 or $150,000,000 upon a railway and then rent it at 3 per cent for fifty years, when very likely we shall have to pay 5 per cent or 6 per cent for the money with which to build it. I do not think I am misleading the House or the country when I make the statement that the government are face to face with a very serious financial difficulty, and they are running their heads against it more and more every day. Take these votes that we are now passing-$13,000,000 of subsidies to railways. We are not going to give these people cash; you are going to give them the credit of the country, and they will go into the financial market and raise money upon that credit. Of course, you say $13,000,000 is only a small matter. But you have several times $13,000,000 that you are guaranteeing, and you have millions coming due that you have to provide for. I think it time to call a halt, as the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) says. We are here to criticise, but the government are here to act. Their actions at the present time are not creditable to themselves as managers of the financial affairs of this country. They have debts to meet, yet they are going on increasing their indebtedness for the sake of subsidizing constituencies and pleasing gentlemen who are going back for re-election. It is very, very serious; and I wish to say to this House through you, Mr. Chairman, that, as a business man, one not brought up to politics or in the atmosphere of politics, that I feel very seriously the position that the government are rushing this country into at the present time. I know that it is unpopular to go to the people, as we expect to have to go, and have it said that we have opposed the expenditure of money in their county. But I say that that is the most contemptible'kind of politics. And I am astonished that a gentleman occupying the position before this country that the Postmaster General does, should be willing to make the reply he did to the hon. member for South Grey and the hon. member for Halton. Their remarks are such as have been called for, loudly called for. by the people for years past. The evidence that such words needed to be spoken is seen in the very votes that we have been passing. These subsidies were voted years ago, yet the promoters of these railways have not been able to raise the money^ over and above the subsidies, to

build roads. I know that from the province of British Columbia, and from what some Reform politicians at one time called the shreds and patches of confederation,' the cry comes for money. And we have eyer been willing to grant that money, so long as it was to be spent solely in the public interest, to build up every part of the Dominion, including these shreds and patches. I do not call them that, for we on this side have always had sympathy with every part of the Dominion, from end to end. We are even in full sympathy with this ' rolling back of the map,' spoken of the other day by the opening up of the northern regions of Canada, if it can be shown that there is anything practical in what the government propose.
But why need they be afraid to put it off till the end of the session ? Why not have (the surveys made and bring down a busC ness system, not mountains of information, by which we are absolutely humbugged ? We want information by prominent engineers. By our course with regard to these transportation systems, we are making ourselves a laughing stock from one end of the country to the other in the financial markets of the world ; we are making ourselves ridiculous by proposing schemes without knowing anything about them, floating them on the market to the detriment of a great many schemes that would ibe beneficial to this country. Each one of these schemes has a certain bearing upon the others. If we go to the financial markets of the old country, or of this country, or of New York, and they ask ns : What are you going to do with this eighty millions of money ? Why, we are going to build a railway from Moncton through to Quebec, and from Quebec to Winnipeg, on a line 200 or 300 miles north of civilization. Well, that is a big scheme, what kind of information have you to go upon ? Well, the Premier of the Dominion of Canada, a gentleman for whom we all have great respect, says tbait he has mountains of information, and lie has brought them down. We find them in a little pamphlet that is perfectly ridiculous. Under these circumstances, I join with my hon. friends from South Grey (Mr. Richardson) and from Halton (Mr. Henderson) in appealing to the government on the general principle. The Postmaster General says : I bring down a vote for so much money that is going to Centre Toronto, and if you dare to vote against it I will leave you in the hands of your constituents. Mr. Chairman, he dares the wrong man.
I will vote against anything that I consider is wrong. I may make mistakes, no doubt I have made a great many, but there is one mistake I won't make, I will not lay before the great financiers of Great Britain, of Canada and of the United States such a scheme as has been propounded by the government without one single particle of information. I say here advisedly that there Mr. BROCK.
is not one member of the government who knows anything at all about that country, not one who has any information from a man that does know anything about building a railway with a grade of four-tenths of one per cent per mile, and with this magnb fieent want of curves. All the grades and curves are in the imagination of the government, who want to discover something to save them from the contempt of this whole country. What have they done ? They have never, since they have been in power, done anything but to go back on thdir records. The Postmaster General knows they have no policy, and those hon. gentlemen whom they took to their bosoms seven years ago have finally become disgusted with them, and they know it. Therefore, I contend that when the Postmaster General gets up to lecture an old member of this House like my hon. friend from Halton, lie makes one of the mistakes of his life. The hon. member for Halton is known to this House and to this country as a safe man. He has advocated no wild cat schemes in this country, but, as an old and prominent business man, he lias asked the government to halt.
Now, with the old votes revoted and the new votes we are asked to pass, we are entering upon an expenditure ol' several millions of dollars. I have looked through these items and I do not see a vote for the Quebec bridge-another very important matter that should be discussed by this House. We are led up to these things little by little, not all at once ; we get them in small homeopathic doses, which gradually approach to allopathic doses ; and I think that by the time we get the big bonuses all through, the country will not put up with it. But the great mistake, I contend, is made in the Railway Committee of this House. We are all at fault on both sides. We give charters to individuals to whom we would not lend a dollar bill ; we give charters to a number of people because some genial member from British Columbia or somewhere else comes forward and jollies us into giving the charter. Now, that is altogether wrong. I contend that this great transportation commission that was heralded with such flourish of trumpets by the Finance Minister should pass upon every one of these charters before they come before the Railway Committee and see whether they are for the general advantage of Canada. Then again these charters should not be granted unless there is some reasonable financial ability behind them to carry them out. Before granting a charter we want to know what bonuses are being granted by the Dominion, by the provincial government and by the municipalities. These are matters so serious that I make no apology in taking up the time of the House in discussing them, even in these last days of the session. These are matters that should be discussed from one end of this country to

the other. It is generally thought that politics is a very different thing from business. When we come here to transact the business of the country we should do it upon the same principles of honour that we transact our private business. I contend that the same principles of justice and right should guide us in the conduct of the affairs of the country as should guide us in the conduct of our individual affairs. What is there more important than drawing upon the revenues of this country, in taking money out of the pockets of the people and using it for public purposes '? In such a serious matter we should exercise the same prudent business principles, the same ideas of rectitude, that we desire to use in the conduct of our private business. We should not be deterred from so doing by the threats of the Postmaster General or anybody else, that we are flying in the face of our constituents if we vote against this or that railway subsidy. I say we must rise above that kind of consideration if we are going to fulfil the national destiny which has been so graphically described by the Prime Minister. I desire to place myself on record along with my hon. friends from South Grey and from Halton, on the general principle which they have* advocated. Let us once settle down upon some safe and just general principle, and we cannot go far astray in details. But when we attempt to do what is fair and just, and dare to express our opinions on the floor of this House, are we to be told by the Postmaster General that we are opposing the interests of our constituents in holding back railway subsidies from them 1 If I thought for one moment that I was sent here to advocate subsidies or anything else for my constituents that were coming out of the pockets of the rest of the people, I would not remain here. I think there is nothing so contemptible as to be continually scheming to get something for your constituents at the expense of other people. I contend there is too much of that kind of thing going on. We have voted this afternoon subsidies, I believe, covering in the vicinity of 4,000 miles of railway. Besides that, I am given to understand that we have got to make arrangements about the Quebec bridge. We have not got that before us yet, but I wish to include that in the protest I am making. Whatever is going to be done must be dione above board, and in the face of the whole country. It must not be done seemingly for one interest when it is in reality for another. Mr. Chairman, I may not have another privilege of addressing you here. I wish now to enter my protest generally against the policy of this government, against the system upon which railway bonuses are granted, upon which bridges are built, railways are built and harbours are subsidized from one end of this country to the other. We are within a few days of the end of the session, when in all probability hon. gentlemen opposite are preparing to appeal to the country
for support or for condemnation, and I desire to take this last opportunity of placing my views on record.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) addresses his remarks to a criticism of what he describes as the general system of bonusing. The general system of bonusing is not the question before the committee. The subject before the committee relates to a number of separate propositions to grant aid to certain railways, some in existence and some not yet in existence. He joins with the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) and the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) in protesting against these subsidies. May I ask the hon. gentleman if he objects to all of the subsidies that are proposed here ?

I think I was pretty plain.
I believe that every subsidy that comes before the House should first of all come before the transportation commission appointed by the right lion, leader of the government.

This is a very large committee. This is a Committee of the Whole House and supersedes all the other committees in Canada in dealing with these propositions at this stage. The hon. gentleman dare not answer that question categorically. He knows that he himself has been pressing the government to grant aid to a railway this session. He knows that he has a mandate from the city of Toronto to use his best endeavours to promote the granting of a subsidy to the James Bay Railway and other railways to aid the city of Toronto. The hon. gentleman will not deny that.

I mean to say that I have no such mandate, and that I have made no such demand. I will always support the granting of a bonus to a railway through a new country, but I would never ask for a bonus for Toronto to secure the building of a railway into that city-never. The city of Toronto got a charter to build a railway. Their experts went up into the James Bay country, through which hon. gentlemen opposite talk of building a transcontinental railway, they found it an impossible country to build through and they dropped it. I know the threat. You need not be at all alarmed about that. I am prepared to say that I would oppose the granting of a subsidy for any railway to be built from Toronto up to the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway.

The hon. gentleman stated in this House on a certain occasion that he was one of a commission appointed by the city council to-consider the scheme of constructing a railway from Toronto to James bay or in that vicinity. He made a mistake on that occasion, because he gave this House to understand that the commission's report was adverse to that scheme. A delegation com-

posed of the city council and the leading citizens of Toronto to a very large number came down to Ottawa-interviewed the government and presented the correct version of what occurred
I

I do not want to misrepresent the hon. gentleman, and he will correct me if I do.
