We were told by this committee composed of the mayor and the leading representatives of the city, the persons who were voicing the views of the city of Toronto, that the events in connection with the commission were not such as the hon. gentleman's recollection led him to think them to be, but that when the commission had presented their report to the city council, the city council were so enamoured of the proposition which had been made that they directed that steps should be taken to obtain an Act of incorporation and to proceed with the scheme of building the James Bay Railway. That is the statement which was made to the government by the mayor and the city council and the leading citizens in the city of Toronto.
Why was it not built ?
That -delegation was heard about six months ago.
This was three or four years ago.

We cannot build a railway in six weeks. They pressed upon the government the advisability of aiding a railway from the city of Toronto northerly to intersect the Canadian Pacific Railway in the vicinity of Sudbury. That request from the hon. gentleman's constituents was made to this government, we have given effect to that view, and I ask the hon. gentleman if it is not fair that he should either join with us in supporting that proposition or put himself on record against it ?
I put myself most positively on record against it.
Against that proposal ?
Against the proposal to build to James bay.

I am speaking of the scheme before the committee. There is a proposition before the hen. gentleman and he may vote for or against it, and that is to build a railway which may be called the James Bay Railway, but which is to aid a railway to be -constructed from the city of Toronto proceeding northerly to Sudbury, and a few miles north of it, perhaps a dozen or twenty miles north. It is in the direction of a line which will ultimately connect with the [DOT]Grand Trunk Pacific. Is the hon. gentleman for or against the granting of a subsidy to Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
the James Bay Railway or to some other railway from Toronto either to intersect the Canadian Pacific Railway in the vicinity of Sudbury, or to be continued northerly until it meets the Grand Trunk Pacific V Would the hon. gentleman kindly give me his opinion on that question ?
Go on and make your speech and I will reply.
Very well. Of course, if the hon. gentleman says that he does not again seek to represent the city of Toronto, that he has no regard for public opinion in Toronto, it does not matter.
I did not say anything of the kind.
I am asking whether we are to take the views of those citizens who came here claiming to represent the opinions of the people of Toronto, or whether we are to take his views.
You can please yourself. You have your choice.

The hon. gentleman has told us his opinion of the proposition that is now before the committee. This is not a fague scheme. It is definite. It is not dealing with an abstract proposition. It is not dealing with a system, but it is dealing with a project to construct a railway from Toronto to Sudbury. .
The scheme is not before me.
I will refer the hon. gentleman to item No. 39.
It is time to take it up when we come to it.

To the James Bay Railway Company for a line of railway from Toronto, via the east side of Lake Simcoe. Parry Sound and Sudbury, towards James bay, not exceeding 265 miles, in lieu of two subsidies granted by chapter 8 of 1900, of 35 and 20 miles respectively, from Parry Sound towards James bay.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. The hon. Postmaster General is discussing a specific item which is on the paper, but which we have not yet reached, and concerning which the hon. Minister of Finance has made no explanation. I would like your ruling.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee commenced deliberations after dinner, I stated that we were now entering upon the consideration of new subsidies, and that the hon. member who rose before six o'clock to engage in a general discussion upon them would be at liberty to do so. I regard this as a general discussion upon the principle of granting subsidies, and I take it that if any particular item is referred to

it is simply referred to as an illustration of the general principle.

Then, Mr. Chairman, prosecuting this inquiry a little further, permit me to say that the city of Toronto has expressed a desire that the government shall aid the Irondale and Bancroft Railway in the extension of its line westward. Is the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) in favour of our listening to the prayer of the city of Toronto in that respect ? There are some others of a like nature that are in the interests of the city of Toronto, and which the city pointedly asked for. I think the city is interested in what is known as the Pembroke Railway, a railway that will ultimately connect the Pembroke Railway with the Toronto system. Toronto is also interested in what is known as the Bobcaygeon and Pontypool Railway, and Toronto is interested in several of these railways under consideration.
In what way is the city of Toronto interested ?
They will help to bring traffic to the city of Toronto.
Financially they are not interested in the building of these roads.

They are desirous of having these roads prosecuted and built, and thus you will see that a very considerable portion, probably one-tenth of the mileage which is to be aided, is in respect of railways that are centering in Toronto or leading towards Toronto, and yet we have an hon. gentleman representing one of the ridings of that city making a general protest against subsidies. Are we not entitled to know where he stands in regard to those particular subsidies for which his constituency is asking ?
Just where I stand iy regard to all other subsidies for railways which are not in the new sections of the country.

I suppose he will then be in the same position as the other members whose constituencies are sufficiently served with railways and who have become virtuous and economical; until his city is so situated, I presume he will support these particular subsidies. 1 will say to him that the government is in favour of the subsidies that are here mentioned and if the hon. gentleman is against these subsidies it is his duty in fairness, and in vindication of that declaration of courage which he says he possesses, to put himself on record, yes or no, for or against these particular subsidies. Until he has done that I say that he has failed to take the only effective course of putting himself on record. He will not find any support for such a resolution on his side of the House. The hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) for example, would differ from him. The hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gour-ley) would differ from him; he is an enterprising gentleman, and so we could run the gamut of the members and they would all vote for the subsidies that are given to help their own constituencies. Perhaps they will not vote for others, but the country is entitled to know where they stand on each proposal. We are not discussing an abstract proposition here, but a particular proposal, to do or not to do something; it is not a mere academical discussion, but a question of contributing public moneys towards certain public enterprises. Each one of these proposals is separate and distinct from the others and it is quite competent for the hon. gentleman to support some and to vote against others. But the country is entitled to know which, if any, of these the hon. gentleman favours or opposes. Toronto particularly is entitled to know from him frankly and fairly whether he is supporting or opposing this scheme, and I will ask him now whether he will take the responsibility on behalf of the city of Toronto of standing up here in this House and requesting the government to strike out all the subsidies for which the city of Toronto has asked.

4 think that nothing more contemptible has ever been performed in this country than the speech which has just been made by the Postmaster General. He asks are all the subsidies in which Toronto has any interest whatever to be struck out. What do you mean ? Toronto is interested in every subsidy that is granted to every railway from the North Pole to the American line. Toronto is cosmopolitan but Toronto is not prepared to advise the government or to advise itself to vote for subsidies for railways not only those in which Toronto has no interest, but simply those in which political knavery alone has an interest. The hon. Postmaster General is not doing himself any credit by the way in which he is attacking me in this matter. He knows what my opinion is in regard to the granting of subsidies and I have stated my opinion very positively to my constituents, that no grant of subsidies ought to be made in the thickly settled parts of this country. But when a grant is made to a railway in British Columbia, Toronto has to pay her share and a very large share it is. Do I object ? No, I do not object to building railways through the sparsely settled districts and Toronto is ready to pay her share, but Toronto has not asked, at least not officially, to build a railway from Toronto north to Lake Simcoe. The hon. Postmaster General thinks that in a very clever and politic way he is going to force me into a corner. He is much mistaken; the country know him and know the petty means and petty kind of politics to which he is willing to descend in the effort to place a political opponent in a corner. I

am not afraid of any corner into which hon. gentlemen opposite can shove. I went into Centre Toronto in the face of a very large adverse majority and of every influence that every member of the two governments, federal and provincial, could bring against me. X had a gentleman opposing me on the platform with a judgeship in his pocket, but the electors turned his majority into a majority for myself. The threat of the hon. Postmaster General has no influence with me at all, and I would be very glad indeed if he dared to come into Centre Toronto and meet me there. 'I will meet him and every argument he can advance in Centre Toronto in any constituency of Toronto. I do not go into York because I suppose that I would have to pose as a farmer there, but even so I would not be very much afraid of him. notwithstanding several great advantages which he possesses, financially and otherwise, tin the attempt he has made this afternoon to corner me he has made a mistake. I stand where I stood before my constituents and say that I oppose subsidies to railways through thickly settled districts, but that I will support subsidies given to railways to open up new territories for Canada.

I think the Postmaster General was hardly fair to the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson). He challenged the hon. member for South Grey to oppose his individual resolutions because there was an application or petition from Grey asking that a railway should be subsidized that was calculated to help that district. The hon. member for South Grey, as he had a perfect right to do, took exception to certain features of the government's policy. He complained of the lateness in the sqsison of the bringing down of these resolutions. There are seventy-eight resolutions here, although there are not seventy-eight railways being subsidized, and the hon. member bad a right to criticise the general policy without attacking any particular resolution. The contention of the hon. Postmaster General was that the hon. member for South Grey, or the hon. member for Halton, or the hon. member for Centre Toronto, had no right to oppose this in a general way, but could only successfully oppose the government's policy in this regard by opposing every individual resolution. The Postmaster General opposed the hon. member for South Grey because he said there was an application from his own county and answered him by saying that it is the case with him as with many others, after a constituency has been liberally supplied by railway subsidies, then the people of that constituency oppose other subsidies. Is that the case with the county of Grey, one of the largest and best settled districts in the province, with 78.000 inhabitants ? Is it a fact that it was liberally subsidized by this parliament ? All the subsidies which that county ever got from this parliament
covered only twenty-eight miles of railway, at the rate of 83,200 a mile.
Where did the rest come from ?

From the municipalities aud the provincial government, chiefly from the municipalities. There were only two short sections subsidized by this parliament in that county ; 13J miles from Owen Sound to Hepworth, and 14 or 15 miles of the Grand Trunk Railway from the county line of Simcoe to Meaford, which was built before confederation. Although the county of Grey is a large county, there is only one railway running through it, and two others touch it ; so that it has not been liberally supplied with railways, and it would not be unfair if the people of that county asked for a little additional aid. The hon. gentleman complained because the hon. member for South Grey took the position he did. That hon. gentleman represents an agricultural constituency, and I respectfully submit that it was eminently his duty to voice the sentiment of his constituents on this subject. His constituents are farmers. If you take up the ' Farmers Sun ' for the past year, which fairly voices the sentiments of the agriculturists of this country, you will find that it has distinctly and consistently opposed the subsidizing of railways by the government. It is ti-ue, there is an application from the county of Grey for a subsidy for a railway-the very next item which we are to take up ; and I can only say that while in the main the people of the country are opposed to railway subsidies, it is a fact that certain localities have not yet been very liberally supplied with railways, and are quite willing to receive assistance from the government to build them ; and it would not be unnatural or unreasonable for the people of the county of Grey to entertain the same views as the people of other sections of the country that are not yet supplied* I may say that I intimated to the government that I was in favour of assistance being granted to that railway. I did so because I know the conditions and circumstances, and I believe it is proper that assistance should be given, in view of the fact that we are assisting railways all over the country, and that the county of Grey has not yet a good supply. Were I to voice the sentiments of the people of Ontario today, I would oppose entirely the granting of railway subsidies ; but I have never gone that far. I believe we ought to discriminate. I believe there are localities for which the government would be justified in subsidizing railways. But in many cases subsidies are given for localities which are already more than supplied. I have always held that the newer sections of the country and localities not already supplied with the conveniences of railways might properly receive government aid for the purpose of obtaining railway facilities. I have endeavoured to discriminate to that extent.

The Postmaster General contended that every member of the opposition who does not by a resolution and vote oppose every item he objects to. tacitly acquiesces in it. That is not a fact. Is an opposition expected to challenge every item in the estimates and have a vote upon it. If so, parliament instead of sitting six months, would sit twelve months in the year. That is not the duty of the opposition. Its duty is to crystallize its policy in an abstract resolution if you like, and vote on that. That conveys the policy of the opposition just as forcibly as though they opposed every single item to which they objected.

I cannot let this opportunity pass without calling the attention of the courageous Postmaster General to some of his attitudes in the past. The hon. gentleman has taken the very opposite courses on more than one occasion in this House. He is very courageous now when he wants to challenge the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) to tell just the precise number of miles of railway construction to which he is opposed. There was a time when the hon. gentleman and his leader had grave fears that the money voted for railway subsidies was stolen and went into an election fund. I want to ask the hon. gentleman if he will vote for a resolution that was proposed in this House in 1894, when a large batch of railway subsidies came down ? Did he ever protest against any railway grant ? The hon. gentleman, I am sure, will give a deaf ear to a suggestion of that kind. Does the lfon. gentleman lay down a course of conduct for this side of the House which he himself refused to pursue in opposition ? Does the hon. gentleman think that a fair or manly game of politics ?	1 do not think he will say that
it is. There is nothing more idle than for an hon. member on either side of the House to get up and challenge the other side to do what he himself refused over and over again to do. But that is what the Postmaster General does. I am coming now to the hon. gentleman's nightmare about the possible pillage of the public treasury by those who received railway subsidies in the past ; and, if he has not become more honest himself or if he does not regard others as more honest, if I propose the same resolution to-night, I would have his support. If it was a good proposition then, it is an equally good proposition now. This is the resolution that was proposed in this House by no less a person than the Prime Minister, and that was supported energetically by the Postmaster Gerferal with the ability he displays when he is wrong, though I will assume he was right on that occasion.
Mr. Laurier moved that the said resolutions he not now read the second time, but that they he referred hack to committee to consider the following amendment :-
That within four days after the opening of each session, the Minister of Railways shall lay
upon the Table of the House, copies of all agreements made by any of the companies with the government together with a statement of all payments made by the government up to date, for subsidies earned by any of the said companies, and the Orders in Council authorizing such payments.
That within a month after the payment to any company of any portion of the subsidies, the president and manager of said company shall furnish to the Auditor General a statement under oath showing if the whole of the subsidies so paid to the company have been applied in the manner herein intended, and that a similar statement shall be supplied by every contractor of the company who is to receive or has received the payment out Of any such subsidies or out of the proceeds thereof, and that, within four days after the opening of each session, the Auditor General shall lay all such statements upon the Table of the House.
That all such documents thus laid upon the Table of the House shall be referred to the Committee on Public Accounts to be by them investigated in the same manner as the public accounts.
That every officer and director of the said companies and every person having a contract with any of the companies for the performance of any work, the doing of anything, or the furnishing of any goods, effects, or materials, and having or expecting to have any claim or demand against the company by reason of such contract, who either directly or indirectly, by himself or by any person on his behalf, subscribes, furnishes or gives, or premises to subscribe, furnish or give, any money or other valuable consideration for the purpose of promoting the election of any candidate to a legislature or to parliament, or with the intent in any way of influencing or affecting the result of a provincial or Dominion election-is guilty of a misdemeanour and liable to a fine of not less than one hundred dollars and not exceeding one thousand dollars ; unless the value of the amount or thing paid, offered, given, loaned, promised, received or subscribed, as the case may be, exceed the last mentioned sum, in which case the fine may be raised to a sum not exceeding such value, and also to a term of imprisonment not exceeding one year and not less than one month, and in default of payment of such fine, to imprisonment for a further term not exceeding six months.
My hon. friend the Postmaster General supported that in a very vigorous speech. I ask him now if he is prepared to characterize as a farce both the motion of the Prime Minister and my hon. friend's speech in support of it ? Would he support such a resolution now ? The hon. gentleman will not answer.
When the hon. gentleman takes his seat I will answer.

The hon. gentleman would scarcely repeat the farce he acted on that occasion. He then pretended to believe and sought to make his friends believe, inside and outside of this House, that the money which was voted for railway subsidies during that period was diverted in part to other purposes, that a portion of it went into the hands of individuals for the purpose of controlling the elections and securing the

return of government candidates. Will' he say that the danger is less great now than it was then ? If not, I shall be curious to ascertain whether he would be prepared to support such a resolution coming from this side now ?

I did not hear the whole resolution. I tried to listen to it, but could not catch it all. The hon. gentleman asked me if I would endorse its leading principle, namely, that companies or directors should be prevented from using government bonuses or aid for election purposes. That is the point the hon. gentleman puts.
The point I put is the resolution.

I did not hear the whole of the resolution. When he came to that part of it, he asked me if I would vote for such a resolution. All I have to say is that since that time we have enacted a statute which covers that groan . by making It penal for directors to contribute to election funds.
That is not all. The hon. gentleman has, when he likes, very acute hearing. And he must remember in any case what resolution he voted for.
I voted for so many.

The hon. gentleman voted for so many absurd resolutions that he is now trying, not to remember them, but to forget them. One part of that resolution declared that the accounts should be audited by the Public Accounts Committee and investigated in every case.
What was the view of the government of that day on that point ?
The view was that the hon. gentleman had moved an absurd resolution.
Then surely my hon. friend would not ask me to do an absurd thing and vote for an absurd resolution ?

I ask him to recall his absurdity or repeat it. I am not saying that the resolution should have been moved, but I am pointing to the part which the hon. gentleman then played. If my memory serves me right, a resolution was passed at the Liberal convention, held in this city in 1893. declaring that no bonuses or subsidies should be granted to railways.
There never was any such resolution passed.

I am speaking subject to correction. I think there were speeches made in that direction. But resolutions never did bind these hon. gentlemen. The very resolution I have just read does not bind him in any way, and I only read it for Mr. CLANCY.
the purpose of calling his attention to the absurd course he took in the past. It was then urged that it would be very dangerous to mix up railway matters with the Criminal Code, and the then Minister of Justice pointed out that the resolution was an absurd one. Coming to the general railway resolutions before us, I desire to say that we have reached a time in the history of Canada when we may well consider whether we are to continue a policy of granting aid to every railway in Canada, long or short, no matter what the conditions may be. There is no hon. gentleman on either side who will not say that we are living under very different conditions now to those existing twenty years ago, and therefore a policy which might have been pursued in the past to advantage might be an unwise policy today. I am not prepared to say that it was at any time a proper policy to vote aid indiscriminately to every railway, whether meritorious or not. There may be some cases in which, in a growing country such as this, it would be very proper to give aid to railways, but the general principle ought to be just the other way. We should only provide for the exceptional cases, and not lay down a broad policy which, as my hon. friend from Ilalton (Mr. Henderson) has pointed out, can have but this result, that not one mile of railway will ever be built without a subsidy. In my judgment, that is going entirely too far. I think we have come to the time when we may well call a halt, and treat the subsidizing of railways as the exception and not-the rule. I have no doubt that some of the grants proposed in these resolutions will aid colonization roads and accomplish a very good purpose. I have not less doubt that there are other cases that are not sufficiently meritorious to justify us in assisting them from the public treasury. When the hon. gentleman tells us that we must point out the particular railway we are opposed to, and not only that, but how much we are opposed to it, he is laying down a rule that he would not follow himself ; and if any one shows a lack of courage, it is one who lays down for others a rule which he would shrink from having applied to his own conduct.

I listened with some astonishment to the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mu-lock) in his cross-examination of the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr, Brock). I notice that his cross-examination took place in the absence of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright). Those who recollect the days of other Liberal leaders and other Liberal principles, I think, will share my astonishment at that cross-examination. Should the Postmaster General ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce such questions, or summon to his chamber Hon. Edward Blake, and subject him to a similar cross-examination, the answers they would give would be

very interesting, I am sure, to the whole committee. If he should ask Mr. Blake what he thought of this policy of government subsidies to local railways, that gentleman would tell him-if he has not entirely gone back on his old principles-that they were absolutely unconstitutional, that it was contrary to the British North America Act to spend a dollar of federal money on local railways. And lion, gentlemen who followed Mr. Blake at that time agreed with him to a man; and they are recorded in the journals of this House as agreeing to that principle which he put in the form of a resolution and proposed as the Liberal view. That would be Mr. Blake's opinion. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has never recanted, so far as I am aware-except by his silence now giving consent to the government proposition-the very terse description he gave of this sort of policy. When dealing with votes for railway subsidies brought down by the government of the day, though for a good deal smaller amount than these, he stated that each and every one of these votes was a bribe to the constituencies, that these railway subsidies were mere rat holes for public money. I think that would have been a very interesting addition to the examination of the Postmaster General. And, perhaps, before these resolutions are carried we may be able to carry on the system of the Postmaster General and have the privilege of cross-examining the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the subject and see whether he maintains his former attitude. And this reminiscence is rather interesting too for another reason. I think a large number of gentlemen on this side of the House still favour the principle that was put in force by the Conservative government and bitterly opposed at the outset by the Liberal party. JIany of these subsidies are for railways in districts already supplied with railway accommodation, and so not of such a nature as those proposed when the principle was introduced. It is interesting to observe these gentlemen coming down with such magnificent figures and such generosity, after the years that have elapsed and the work that has been done. I think there is a great deal of room for criticism in regard to the carrying out of that policy in certain portions of the province of Ontario. But I am sure that in other provinces on the Atlantic and the Pacific, the quarrel with the government will be-and I am frank to say it-that they have 'not been sufficiently generous. I do not think the people there would be opposed to this principle if it were applied properly. And, I think the contrast between the policy of the Liberal government and the policy of the Conservative government is that, under the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, the. outlying portions of the Dominion do not receive the consideration they should receive, consideration that, under the pre-450
sent policy, appears to be given to the older and more settled parts of the country.

I think it might not be amiss to call attention to the fact that there is a good deal of justification for the discussion that has taken place in connection with these railway subsidies. I entirely sympathize and agree with the opinion expressed by my hon. colleague (Hon. Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper) that, so far as some of the smaller and less developed provinces and parts of the Dominion are concerned, there is, to my mind, a demand for some system of railway subsidies. There can be no question about the value of railway construction, and there can be no question that many parts of the country are not supplied with railway facilities as they should be. Nor can there be any question as to the value to these localities and to Canada as a whole from the legitimate and proper expanding of our railway system. But while I believe, that, I believe also that there are objections to the mode in which these subsidies are voted. For instance, we are to-night voting subsidies to a sum the magnitude of which many hon. members do not seem to realize. Take $3,200 a mile as a basis, and allow five per cent additional for the fact that a larger sum is promised to such roads as cost over $15,000 a mile. The mileage here subsidized is 3,928 miles. At $3,200 a mile, this would be $12,569,600. Add to that five per cent, as I have suggested, $628,480, and you find that the total subsidies now before us is $13,198,080.
Does that include revotes ?

Including everything. Here is a sum that we are voting in the course of one evening; and it is more than one-third of a sum which my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) declared not so many years ago was too large to be expended upon all the services of Canada. The time is not remote when the hon. gentleman pronounced $38,000,000 an extravagant sum to be expended on the services of Canada in every direction, and here to-night he and other hon. gentlemen who sympathized with him at that time, many of them associated with the government, are cheerfully and, apparently with a great deal of pleasure and satisfaction, as evidenced by their laughter, voting more than one-third of that sum for railway construction alone, and that in a direction which they cannot fail to remember, they uniformly condemned when in opposition. I do not mean to say that the views of these gentlemen were right when they condemned that course. It seems that they themselves have come to the conclusion that they were mistaken. They have set themselves with great assiduity to reverse their position upon all subjects upon which they expressed themselves. Their conduct during the years they have had a chance to show how they



would really act must convince us tliat tlieir opinions when in opposition do not now meet with their approval. Their conduct now is entirely at variance with those opinions. But we cannot hope that any government or opposition will be altogether wise. The most that we can hope for is that they shall do their best to govern the country honestly and well, and that the opposition will criticise as honestly and capably as they can the conduct of the government in power. Therefore, I do not think there is great profit to be derived from pointing out the fact that the course hon. gentlemen opposite are entering upon with such satisfaction is at variance with their opinions of the past. But at the time when we were to vote railway subsidies to the amount of over $13,000,000, there was an opportunity for the government to consider whether or not this was a proper system and the proper way to aid in the construction of such railway works as are still necessary.
Now to my mind it is a very grave question whether the country gives a sufficient amount of attention to this large portion of our national outlay. It seems to me doubtful if the government has fully and carefully considered whether in following the old method in which the example has been set to them by their predecessors, they are not perhaps continuing a method which might be superseded by a better one. To my mind the great purpose of railway subsidies is the economical construction of railways in portions of the country where they are wanted, and the point that ought to be kept clearly in view is whether any return for the large outlay which the country is asked to make can be expected ; and secondly, whether the localities in which the expenditures are being made will get as much benefit under this system as they might under a different one. Now there was an opportunity at this time, in view of the large extent of these subsidies, to have given a careful consideration to this matter. I think it is to be regretted that there is not evidence to show that the government has studied this subject. I am of the opinion that the government of Canada, instead of subsidizing by a cash bonus, roads at random, in great numbers, which are pressed upon their attention by interested corporations or even by prominent supporters, should have introduced a different method altogether, should have inquired carefully into these several propositions, and only given their support to such railway propositions as conveyed to them a reasonable assurance that they were likely to be carried out successfully at an early period, to all the rest turning for the time being a deaf ear.
I would further suggest that it would be to the advantage of the country if, instead of aiding these selected and favoured railways by a cash subsidy, the government should give their aid in the form of a guar-Mr. BELL.
antee upon a certain percentage of the bonds of the corporations which came to them and asked for support. That system has been to a certain extent adopted this year in the very extensive bonuses which have been promised to the Mackenzie & Mann system in the west, and those which are promised to the Grand Trunk Pacific. In these cases the government have entered upon that course ; instead of giving the cash subsidy we have given a guarantee. To my mind the great point to be kept in view is what the burden upon the country is going to be that will be created by carrying out these railway propositions. If it can be proved, or if it appeared to the satisfaction of the government, that the capital required to complete these railways would be lessened by a government guarantee as compared with the system of giving a cash subsidy in aid of these roads, then I think it would be better for the country and better for the localities in which these roads are built that the former principle should be substituted. The great purpose that ought to be kept in view is to bring the cost of these public works down to the lowest possible point, and in that way the burden which they subsequently impose upon the locality for which they are constructed and which must be met from the tolls collected by these roads, would be reduced to the lowest point. The result would be that we would derive the benefit of railway construction at the least possible cost, and upon the most advantageous terms. Now here was a great opportunity, because we are spending a very large amount of money, we are bonusing nearly eighty different lines of road over every part of Canada; and here was a great opportunity for the government to give this matter full consideration, and if they were satisfied that a better system could be discovered, to have introduced that system. There is not, I regret to say, any evidence before us to show that the government has bestowed any great amount of study upon this question. Therefore, to my mind, they have lost a valuable opportunity for giving very full and careful consideration to this matter.
Then again there is this to be said. This vote, aggregating over $13,000,000, is introduced at a time of the session when it cannot receive the discussion which this kind of expenditure, with the burden which it is imposing upon the country, would seem to warrant. These resolutions might have been much better introduced at an earlier period of the session, when they could have been fully and carefully discussed. There is no question to-day of more importance to this country than that of railway construction. We know' that we have to build in the course of a few years to come, a great many miles of road all over Canada. We know we must do that, therefore, it is to my mind, most important that if we are'not proceeding upon the best possible course

we should turn from that course and adopt a better one at the earliest moment.! It is idle to expect this time to engage in a discussion extending over a week or two weeks of time that might be required in order to thresh this subject out thoroughly, to collect all the necessary information, and to arrive at a satisfactory and final decision upon this question. I say we cannot hope to have that at this stage of the session ; therefore, I regret that these resolutions have been brought down at so late a period.
That brings to my mind what is perhaps the strongest objection, from all points of view, to such resolutions as we have before us to-day. I regretted very much the tone and substance of the speech made by the. Postmaster General to-night. I regretted it, because I saw a manifest disposition on his part to make prominent a feature in this discussion that to my mind is not creditable to this parliament, and that is his assumption that members of parliament in voting upon these resolutions are not free agents, that they are not giving to this subject their best judgment, their independent judgment ; that they are voting, on the other hand, entirely in the fear of their constituents in every case in which the constituents of any member are interested parties. That may well be the case. To be perfectly frank, in these railway subsidies there are votes in which my constituents are interested, and which I would, if necessity required, support with my vote. In respect of these matters, I feel that I have a mandate here to support these particular resolutions. Every other gentleman in this House whose constituents are interested in a particular vote, must feel the same stress. I do not like to see that, in this matter, the government are relying upon what can be called nothing else than log-rolling on a gigantic scale, in depending for support of hon. gentlemen in this House because each one of them is interested in one or more of the resolutions. It is practically organizing a log-rolling operation on a wholesale system for the government of the day to bring in seventy or eighty resolutions and rely for their passage upon the fact that individual members of the House on both sides are interested in one or more of these resolutions, and therefore, will vote for the whole lot because each one is interested in one or more. It is not seemly to make that idea prominent, and to my mind it is not fair. It is not to the advantage of the people that the independence of members of the House should be lost from the fact that their constituencies are interested in one or more of these resolutions. To my mind, if these resolutions cannot receive tne sanction of the independent judgment of individual members, then that is a great reason why they should not be introduced at all. They should not be brought down in batches and voted through simply because individual members cannot oppose some of them and 450J
therefore have to accept them all. There is a further serious objection. There can be no question that, to a certain extent, while the objects for which these votes are made,, while the purpose for which this money is being asked and received is laudable, nevertheless in the mode, and manner, and selection of these subsidies, the government in giving to the several corporations interested has a direct opportunity for the exercise of political interference in favour of the government. For instance, to-night we have nearly eighty railway resolutions brought down in one session ; at the last session of parliament not one was introduced.
There cannot be any one in this House who would argue that there was absolutely no necessity for these railways last year and an overpowering necessity this year. It is perfectly clear that the voting of money in this particular fashion places it in the hands of the government of the day to bestow great largesses upon great corporations and people at such times as they think they can bestow those largesses to the best advantage to themselves. This to my mind gives an opportunity to the government of the day to exercise enormous political influence and therefore it is not to the advantage of the country that it should be done in that way. It may be to the advantage of this government but it is not to the advantage of the country. One may say that if the country were entirely opposed to that 'mode of doing business, it would show it, in the manner in which it would receive these votes or proposals and that until there is such a body of independent opinion among the electors who are not favourable to the exercise of political pressure by the government in this fashion we may expect to see things go on as they are going. But, that does not make the matter right. If by this system of giving subsidies at such times and in such a way and under such modes as the government of the day adopts, leads to political influence being exerted on a great scale, I believe that every hon. gentleman will agree with me in saying that it is a bad thing, that it is not in the interests of the people of the country, that it is not in the interest of the government and that it will not have a tendency to strengthen the parliament of Canada. Generally speaking we must be favourable to the development of our railway system and I am prepared to support the government of the day in extending our railway system. I maintain that there are large portions even of the older provinces where we must have a great and rapid extension of the railway system if we are going to have a rapidly developing population and a rapid increase in wealth but I think it is an unfortunate thing that successive governments should bestow large sums of money in the form of subsidies when the individual members of those governments while sitting on the opposite side of the House had previously opposed

them all through. If expenditures that are wrong in the view of successive oppositions are going to be right in the . view of successive governments, then I say that there can be no question in the mind of any reasonable man that our system is not such a system as we should adopt in a country like this. For that reason X would like very much if the government of the day had introduced these resolutions at an earlier period of the session and if they had brought them down and submitted them to parliament at such a time and with such information as to make parliament feel that a strong case might be made out for a better system of expenditure, one which would be more absolutely free from all suspicion of the desire to exert political influence. I would have welcomed it. I believe it would not be a difficult matter for parliament to devise a method by which we would have the most important work of railway construction carried on more successfully and more economically than it is to-day and at the same time eliminate from the work of carrying on railway construction those objectionable features from which this system should be altogether free. We do not want to have it in the mouths of successive oppositions in this House to say that the ministers of successive governments have been promoting their own ends by the aid of this system, either as individual members of the government or as a party. This is not attaining to the highest possible plane of statesmanship or politics in this country that we can attain to, and in the meantime it will always remain an open question as to whether the governments which do make these large expenditures in the hope of personal advantage are not therein deceived. I am pleased to see that the government is not going to lose sight of the important work of railway construction but it seems to me that I might also express my regret that this enormous expenditure has not been submitted to us at a time when we could discuss it fully with some possibility of arriving at a decision on the subject and with a chance of discovering perhaps some better way in which this expenditure could be made.

There can be no objection, as we are now in committee, that each of these items should be discussed on its merits and there is no reason for alleging that the committee should rise until there has been an ample opportunity given for that to be done. I only rose to point out to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Bell) that if the committee approve of all these subsidies and) they should be granted it is not only improbable, but it is not possible that the $13,000,000 which he says they will cost will have to be paid in any one year. Perhaps they will not be paid in one, two, three or four years. Long lines of railway will take some time to construct and as he knows it is only as ' Mr. BELL.
construction proceeds that they are to be paid. Therefore, he must not look upon it in the light of our incurring a liability which during any given financial year will amount to $13,000,000 and which will have to be defrayed. We must proceed in a businesslike way in developing the country and we are all anxious to see it developed, but, we must at the same time have regard to the revenues of the country and to the ability of the country to carry out these undertakings. There may be schemes other than those proposed which would be in the interest of the country, but you might not be able to accomplish everything in one year. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that some years ago, before the Liberal party came into power, some members of that party took exception to an expenditure of $38,000,000 and said it was time to cry a halt and that there should be economy practised. That is quite true and there was a reason for it. In those days the revenues of the country were not paying the ordinary expenditure and all the works on capital account that were being entered into were being undertaken with borrowed money. Therefore, under these circumstances it was a wise and prudent thing to say that we should be careful, and that we should not proceed as they were proceeding at that time. But what are the conditions now ? Hon. gentlemen opposite know what the position was then and they know what it is now. There have been a great many millions of expenditure made, but the revenue that came in and the revenue that came in under a lower rate of taxation than prevailed in those days
No, no.

A lower rate of taxation than prevailed in those days has sufficed not only to pay the ordinary expenditure of the government, but it has paid the capital expenditure of government and left a surplus ever and above. Therefore, I would feel, such being the condition of things, when trade was stagnant and population not increasing, when the revenue was not sufficient to meet the ordinary expenditures of government, not to speak of doing nothing else, that it was desirable to call a halt, but now, under the changed conditions, when, under a lower rate of taxation, you have a revenue enough not only to pay your ordinary expenditure, but as I have said, to pay all of your capital expenditure, your bonuses for iron and, for railway construction, your expenditure on capital account for canals and other works and something over that besides, hon. gentlemen will see, that, this being the state of things, this government while they are making generous [DOT]expenditures, or rather proposing to parliament that the country is in a position to make generous expenditures, can do that without alarm on sound business principles and that it is a wise principle for

parliament to proceed upon having regard for the resources of the country. They have regard to the development of the country, and they submit their opinions for the judgment of this committee ; they believe in the development of the country in the directions that are indicated that they can do this out of the revenue of the country without entailing burdens on the people, and if our friends opposite will consider the operations of the last few years they will arrive at the same conclusions as we do, and, therefore, I would ask them to look upon the expenditure proposed by the government in the light of the present condition of the country and of its prospective development and advancement. I think they will agree with the government, that while wq are making these expenditures, looking towards the development, nevertheless we are proceeding in a wise, prudent, businesslike way, having regard to the needs and improvements of this country. As to whether the country is in a position to do this or not, for my own part I believe that the country can well afford to do it. I believe the country can meet the obligations parliament is assuming through the legislation of this session without unduly increasing the burdens of the people, and will be able to carry out the great schemes of development that parliament has so far sanctioned or may still sanction.

The junior member for Piet ju (Hon. Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper) said there was a political stress upon members of this House. I agree with that, but I do not agree that the political stress is on this side of the House; the political stress is on the other side of the House. I am a supporter of subsidies. Ever since I entered this parliament and long before, I was a supporter of subsidies, because the Conservative party of this country adopted it as their policy to develop this country by encouraging the building of railways by subsidies. All that I have to complain of is that you gentlemen who adopted that policy along with all the Conservative policies, do not come frankly into this House and confess that you stole that policy. I think you should clothe yourselves with sackcloth and ashes and make a frank, open confession that you have stolen our policy on railways, as you have stolen the national policy and the bounty on iron. If you should frankly acknowledge this, you would escape the censures which people are now passing on you. The repentant sinner who turns in his way is always welcomed by good men, but it is on open and frank confession that he is forgiven. The same generosity would be extended to you here, but you insist upon stirring up ill-will in this House by claiming that you have adopted a policy and that it is your policy. I undertake to say that every dollar of money voted for subsidies in Colchester will inure
to my support, because the electors will say : This is the policy of the Liberal-Conservative party which the Liberals dared not change when they came into power. If the Minister of Finance will give me two or three more subsidies I will get every vote in Colchester, Liberal or Conservative, because the Conservatives will claim for me, and the Liberals will admit it, that by advocating the policy of subsidies I am pursuing the old policy of the Conservative party, which the Liberals have been compelled by public opinion to adopt after attacking it for 18 years. I regard their conduct in doing that as the only satisfactory feature in their whole course. I congratulate them on being strong enough to admit that they were wrong. Some one should move in this House, for the sake of the history of this present generation, to strike out from tbe ' Hansard ' of this country the speeches of gentlemen opposite for the 18 years from 1878 to 1896, because if these speeches are permitted to remain intact they will form the basis for the historian to write the history of this generation, and I am bound to say if he happens in his search for information to light upon the speech of the Minister of Customs, he will decide that in this day and generation we were incompetent imbeciles, because the speeches he made during these 18 years, instead of aiding the progress of Canada, instead of inspiring the young people of this country and creating a feeling favourable to tbe growth of Canada, were intended to cripple the people of this country, especially in the matter of railways. The Conservative party made Canada; they found four little scattei

ed provinces; they united them; then they built tbe Intercolonial, which was the first link between the provinces; then they acquired British Columbia and the west, and pursued their great policy by building the Canadian Pacific Railway. But these were only preliminary steps, and the Conservative party, when they had consolidated Canada into one country went forward and said : We shall have a policy of railway development. They followed that policy continuously in the face of the most determined and unreasonable opposition that was ever offered to a political party in any country, and you gentlemen were the men responsible for that opposition. I in my bumble way down in the country, was supporting railway development, supporting these subsidies when Sir Charles Tupper and Sir John A. Macdonald were advocating them, and the Conservative party also supported them. All I can say is that as you gentlemen have adopted our policy I am bound to go on and support that policy. My bon. friend who sits beside me (Hon. Mr. Ilaggart), when be was Minister of Railways again and again introduced railway subsidies, but he was met and fought step by step as if he were an enemy of the country instead of being one of its great developers and one of its

143S0
great builders. When we pursued a different course in this parliament, I think it is ungenerous for gentlemen to get up and pursue the course that they have done. I for one will say that I support railway subsidies all over the country. Look at the map ! I said a short time ago that we had not commenced the development of Canada.
I said that we had a long fringe of development from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Look at that map ! A little fringe of railways from the Atlantic to the Pacific. But the whole country is as absolutely undeveloped as when the Indians possessed it. There is the evidence that my knowledge was accurate; it is as utterly undeveloped as when the Indians roamed over it, except for a little fringe from ocean to ocean. It is our duty to go forward, developing year by year a vast system of railways, and that is in pursuance of the Conservative policy. I congratulate you, gentlemen, on pursuing that policy. Why do you not be more honest and frank and say : We adopted the Conservative policy of granting railway subsidies; our policy in opposing railway subsidies was all wrong. If you do, there will be no contention on our side. Why don't you tell the truth. You do not tell the truth, and therefore you provoke opposition. I say this because I am anxious to get on with the business of the country. I congratulate the Prime Minister upon having one very frank member of his cabinet; that is the Minister of Trade and Commerce. As soon as the iron bounties were called the Minister of Trade and Commerce gets up and goes out. I think he acted fairly in that ; I am inclined now to believe that the Minister of Trade and Commerce believed in his contentions at the time he made them. I say that the Postmaster General and the Minister of Customs did not believe a word they said ; they were evidently acting a part during these 18 years; they knew they were deceiving the people; they absolutely knew that for IS years, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I am now commencing to believe, honestly believed the nonsense he talked, honestly believed that bounties were an improper policy to pursue in this country. Therefore, whenever the Minister of Finance undertakes to move his resolutions, the old gentleman hobbles out. greatly to his credit. I congratulate the Prime Minister on having one honest, trusty, faithful counsellor on whom he can rely. Even though the doctrines he preached are economically false, he believes them and will stick to them. If the Postmaster General and the Minister of Customs had gone out when these railway resolutions were introduced they would have done themselves a great compliment. They would have shown to us that they disapproved of this railway policy and believed in the policy they had preached for eighteen years. But by sitting here they openly flaunt their indecency, because, after having opposed railway subsidies in every shape Mr. GOURLEY.
and form for eighteen years, they now have the courage not only to support them, but to revile the gentlemen who pursued an honest course. We have the ignoble sight of the notorious sinner reviling the honest patriarch, the representative of truth and right in this country.

Before this discussion is concluded, I wish to enter my protest against this whole bonusing system. I do not agree with the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley), who thinks the country can be built up by bolstering up private interests of one kind and another. A number of gentlemen who spoke to-day have stated that they would gladly support the bonusing system in those parts of the country which are not settled, but would object to it in the more settled parts of the Dominion ; but I cannot find that principle included in the resolutions now before us. They seem to cover the whole country; they seem to make practically no difference between one province and another. In fact, the well-settled districts seem to be more favoured than the unsettled districts ; and when we come down to bonusing railways of one mile in length, it seems to me that we carry the system to an absolute absurdity. There are here about eighty propositions, which I imagine include nearly all the propositions for railway construction in the country at the present time. It would appear to me to be very reasonable to suppose that this system, developed as it has been, actually retards the construction of railways where they are necessary. Where it is decided by a railway company that a line should be constructed as a business proposition, it is not constructed until such time as political influence can be brought to bear to obtain a subsidy ; and therefore the construction of necessary lines is prevented. Now, I do not wish to discuss this matter at any length. I have protested against other bonusing Bills and I protest against this. I think the system is wrong. I look for a better system. It is useless for us to support in bulk or in detail a system that we would rather see abolished, and the country as a whole is opposed to this system. When a proposition is put before us in this way, affecting, as it does, almost every section of the country, it is not to be supposed that you can get a general sentiment expressed against it; but if the principle of bonusing railways could be put before the people of Canada, irrespective of any particular Bill, I do not think any of us could have any doubt what the verdict would be. I therefore oppose this bonusing Bill, not only in bulk, but in detail.
Where is this road to commence and where is it to finish ?
This is an extension of the road referred to in the first item. A portion of the subsidy is revoted, and this is for an extension as described.

That does not answer the question. According to the resolution, it this subsidy is granted, the promoters of the railway will have the right to commence it at Ingersoll and take it to the city of Stratford, a distance of 35 miles. That is one proposition. But if they do not choose to do that, they have the right to commence it at Woodstock and take It to Berlin, which may be a distance of 35 miles ; or they would have the right to commence at either Ingersoll or Woodstock and stop at any point between Berlin and Stratford. I object to this method of granting subsidies, without specifying the starting point or the ending point. It gives the promoters a chance to hold up the different municipalities for bonuses. Can the minister not specify where this company will have the right to commence the road and where they will have the right to finish it ?

I may say, for the information of the committee, that this company have a charter to build from Port Burwell, on Lake Erie, to Collingwocid, on the Georgian bay. They represent that this would be a short and good road for bringing coal from Port Bur-well to the various centres throughout the province of Ontario where there are large manufacturing industries, and for bringing grain from Collingwood to Port Burwell. A portion of the road has been subsidized in the past, and is now running from Port Burwell to Ingersoll. That portion of the subsidy which has not been earned, for about nine miles from Ingersoll to Woodstock, is revoted. The company say that they have not decided which is the best line to take to the Grand Trunk, whether by Stratford or by Berlin, continuing north to Collingwood. The subsidy has been petitioned for by almost all the growing towns throughout that part of Ontario, and the government thought that as that portion of the road from the lake to Ingersoll had been built and was in operation, it might b& well to give the company this slight encouragement. While it will serve local needs to some extent, it is expected to be of more value as a through line.
Is this the road with which the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr; Charlton) is associated ?
I think he is now very considerably associated with the road.
Well, we had better pass that.

Would the Minister of Railways and Canals be good enough to tell the committee whether the petitions ask for a road from Ingersoll to Stratford or from AAroodstock to Berlin ? If this resolution be carried, this railway will have the right to construct the road from AVoodstock to Berlin, or from Ingersoll to Stratford. It is only fair that the company should state
from what point it intends to start, and where it intends to go, rather than have this choice, because this option will enable it to work the municipalities for subsidies by threatening to go in whatever direction it will obtain the largest subsidies. Did the citizens of Stratford petition the government to subsidize a road from Ingersoll to Stratford, and did the citizens of Berlin petition the government to subsidize a road from Woodstock to Berlin 1 The A1INISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. My recollection is that the petitions were in favour of the scheme in a general way. The municipalities to which my hon. friend refers are all very well supplied with railways, and they will get the advantage of this line, no matter in which section of the county it may run. The object is not so much to have a local road as to have coal distributed cheaply to the various manufacturing centres, for it is a matter of very material importance to the manufacturers throughout that section of the country to have their coal delivered as cheaply as possible. Then there is a great deal of the produce of the country originating on the Grand Trunk Railway and the Great AVestern which will be taken by this line, and in that way there will be competing rates from this lake port. The people will find a market they can serve and even have water during a part of the year from Port Burwell to Montreal. These are representations which were made by the company to the municipalities supporting it. As either of these two options will be through the same counties and municipalities, I do not think there will be much danger of any competition with regard to municipal bonuses. That is a matter any way about which we in this House need not have any particular care. If the municipalities are so anxious to have this road and think it will be so great a benefit that they are willing to vote assistance, that is then-own business. But my hon. friend knows that in Ontario the people must be strongly in favour of a public enterprise of this description before they will grant it any bonus. It must be almost the unanimous wish of the electors of any village, town, township or county before any enterpiise of this description will get municipal aid.
This is a road which has been in existence for some time from Port Burwell to Ingersoll.
It is just completed this year to Ingersoll.

Yes, this is intended to be a through road from Port Burwell to Collingwood. You give the option to this road, but it ought to have its plan and it ought to have decided on its route. These parties must know what route they intend to take, and their object must be, in having this option, to go to the different municipalities and say :	' If
you do not give us sufficient bonus and per-

haps right of way or other conditions, we will take it to the other place.' You are giving this company the opportunity of holding up these municipalities for the purpose of getting bonuses. Here is an old road which was built from Port Burwell a number of years ago, now completed to the town of Ingersoll. The company propose to go to Collingwood. Surely they know the route. Why do they not come here and ask for a bonus from one particular point to another and not be allowed the opportunity of holding up the different towns and municipalities along tv., line by saying :	' The
government have given us the option of going anyway we like between these two different points, and we will go in that direction which will give us the largest bonuses.'

I would like very much if possible to have a change made and the original plan adopted. That is grant a bonus in a comprehensive way when you are about it for a railway from Lake Erie to Collingwood. I want to square myself with the Postmaster General and show him that I am not so narrow minded as to oppose all kinds of bonuses. But if we are going to give a bonus, it should be for some comprehensive scheme and not a little patch work such as this. This will be a bonus hunting road. We know who is behind this road, and in that respect it is unlike most of those other schemes that come before us.
I believe that the promoters deserve well of the government and that it would be well to give a bonus of so much a mile right straight through from Ingersoll to Collingwood. In my opinion the country would support such a vote. I agree with the Minister of Public Works that the building of this road will have the effect of laying coal down in the central part of Ontario much cheaper than at present. It will bring coal directly across Lake Erie to Port Burwell and from Port Burwell it would be quite reasonable that we should build this road to a port on the Georgian bay. It has a charter to Collingwood. Then why not at once instead of aiding it in a half hearted way, give it a subsidy from Ingersoll to Collingwood. I would be very sorry that it should go past my hon. friend's home and town, but even if the road should run directly through Ingersoll to Collingwood and not touch at some of the other towns, they are well supplied with railway facilities by the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the Canada Southern. Let this road run through to Collingwood. If a scheme of that kind were to be adopted, this parliament would be justified in granting a bonus all the way and I would ask that that change be made now if possible.
Is this road going to Collingwood, or is it not proposed to change it, and instead of going to Collingwood to make the terminus at some other [DOT]
point ? I understand that, if they go from Woodstock the chances are they will run on to Collingwood, but if they run from Berlin they will go on to the shores of Lake Huron.

I understand-and I go simply by their own representations-that their terminus is Collingwood. My hon. friend (Mr. Brock) will see that, while I live in Woodstock and my interests are there to a great extent, I am not selfish in this matter. Their present subsidy takes them to Woodstock, but they represented to the government that it might be in the public interest as well as in the interest of the company that they should go north by Stratford, as being a somewhat shorter and, perhaps, a better route. I quite agree with that, because, if it is a good enterprise, the shorter the line they can make and the better the grades from Lake Erie to Georgian bay, the better it would be in the interests of the whole country. Therefore, I did not object nor do I now, to their proposal to change their course. If they run ten miles from the town I live in and where my; interests lie, I am sure the hon. gentleman will exonerate me from any personal interest or feeling. If I had told them that they had already intimated that it was their intention to go through Woodstock, that they had been subsidized to that point, and I would not agree to a change, I might then be accused of selfishness. But I frankly told them that, if it were in the general interest and in the interest of the company to go the other way I was satisfied. I can see the force of what the hon. gentleman says that it would be a good thing if encouragement were of fered to the whole scheme from water to water. But the hon. gentleman must remember that this is a very large country, and there are a great many districts that have no railway facilities. And I must say that I, for one, have always supported with a better heart the granting of assistance to a road that was opening up a new section of the country than to one running through a territory already fairly provided with railway facilities. But I am satisfied that, no matter which cf these routes the company take, if they can go on delivering coal at the prices at which they are now delivering it, it would be of as great advantage to the manufacturers of Woodstock as though the road ran directly through the town. If I remember well, they got a subsidy from Port Burwell to Tilsonburg, where they connected with the Michigan Central and with a branch of the Grand Trunk. Then they came back to seeurei powers to connect with the Canadian Pacific Railway. The great roads are interested in lending their assistance and endorsing this proposition, because, as represented to me, they are interested in getting coal for their own use at this point. They are a long distance from the coal fields, and can bring it better in this way

than by a route upon which we spent considerable money-bringing coal by boat to Port Dover and connecting with a branch of the Grand Trunk. But the navigation was not found very satisfactory. If the ideas of the present company are successful, the road will be one of great advantage to the whole of that district of Ontario. If it is (merely a local road I should not be here advocating a subsidy for it.

There is no denying the importance of the road, if it is completed, and I agree with the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) that, if the whole road were subsidized, it would be better, as we should have it completed at au earlier date. But if we cannot get a subsidy for the whole, it is at least well to get a subsidy for a portion of it.
Why not for the whole ? There is an overflowing treasury.

I admit we should be better pleased to have all subsidized, but, if the government see proper to subsidize only a part, that will still be useful. But I want to endorse what the hon. member of Peel (Mr. Blain) said, that the proposition now, so far as I can see, will lead to the holding up of the municipalities. I do not say that I object to the change of route. If you build to Woodstock, you build along side of two other railways ; but, if you go to Stratford, you will go through a section that has no railway just now. It is true, you are not very far from a railway in either case, but the route to Stratford will do more to afford facilities to a new section than will Woodstock. But it is a wrong principle to give a railway company power to hold up the municipalities. We all know what railway corporations are-they 'have neither souls nor bowels of compassion. They take every dollar they can get, and play one municipality off against the other for all they are worth. They should not be allowed an opportunity to do so. This company should not be allowed an opportunity to do so. This company should choose as direct a route as possible to Collingwood and receive a subsidy for that road.

If it would be in order I would like to move an amendment:
That all the words after ' Ingersoll ' be struck out and the following be substituted : * to Collingwood, crossing the Canadian Pacific Railway and Grand Trunk Railway in the most convenient -places and in the most direct way.'

I take it that that amendment; is in order, because it does not propose to increase the amount of the subsidy as I understand it. There is no person here that I know of representing the company. My hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) I had expected to see in the House. I had the information as to this road from him. The solicitor of the company was here at one
time during the session. I fear that the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) would defeat the object the company have in view. Personally, I would have no particular objection tq the amount, but I fear the company could not secure the payment of the subsidy uuder this wording. I think that every hon. gentleman who has had experience in these matters knows of the difficulties that companies have under the wording of the resolutions, even after they have earned their money, in getting payment through the Auditor General. I doubt very much whether that is definite enough. I would have no particular objection to a change, speaking for myself, but I cannot speak for the company. I know they have built the road now as far as Ingersoll. I know the manager of the road, and it has always been represented to me that they had good financial backing. That is proved by the fact that they have completed a somewhat expensive road and equipped it from the lake as far north as Ingersoll. I did not make any particular inquiry with regard to it. I think the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) is financially interested in it. They represented to me that if they built as far as the Grand Trunk they would then he able to supply the Grand Trunk system with a lot of coal. I would be afraid, in changing this without consultation with the solicitor, that we might defeat the object we have in view.

My suggestion was to give them a free hand, but with the distinct understanding that they were to make for Collingwood, and not build to Collingwood. because that is going to be a very different road from the road that is now laid out. A through road of that kind with the prospect of a subsidy is much easier to finance than these little patches of eight or nine miles at a time. If the government could see its way to grant a bonus to this road from Ingersoll through to Collingwood, it would be a great benefit to that country. If it passed by Guelph, or Galt, or Berlin, where there are large factories, it could carry large quantities of coal to these towns. But that should be done with the understanding that the promoters should build it to Collingwood.
I do not think the resolution as drawn could carry out that object.

I understood the acting Minister of Railways to say that the aim of the promoters is to construct it from Ingersoll to Collingwood, with a view of serving that manufacturing section of Ontario with cheaper coal. Now one proposition is to take the line from Ingersoll to Stratford. I want to ask the hon. gentleman if, when it gets to Stratford, it will be as near to Collingwood as when it gets to Ingersoll.
My hon. friend means Berlin or Stratford.
Is Ingersoll closer to Collingwood than Stratford is ?

I am not prepared to say, but looking at the map, there is very little difference. By bearing east in the first place they are going in the direction of Collingwood. If they went due north instead of going to Stratford, they would have to bear east to some other point to reach Collingwood. It would not make any difference in the total mileage.

Ingersoll is nearer to Collingwood than Stratford. If the aim of the promoters of this road is to run a line from Ingersoll to Collingwood, then they are going out of their way when they go to Stratford. A line from Ingersoll to Collingwood in anything like a direct line would not touch Stratford at all. I want to ask the acting Minister of Railways another question with regard to coal. We ail know that a line of railway was subsidized by this government from Port Dover through the central part of Ontario with a view of bringing soft coal from the United States across in boats, connecting at Port Dover with a line of railway running through the province of Ontario to reach these manufacturing points. If I am correctly informed, that venture has proved a dead failure. They have not been able to bring coal across the lake and make connections at Port Dover and serve the central part of Ontario in that way. Now if that be the case, how is it possible to bring coal across Lake Erie to Port Burwell and serve the central part of Ontario with this road, when they cannot do it with the other ? This road has been constructed for many years from Port Bur-well up to Ingersoll, and for a much longer time from Port Burwell to Tilsonburg. Til-sonburg is connected with railways running through all that section of Ontario. What amount of coal has been brought over across Lake Erie to Port Burwell and along this line of railway to Tilsonburg, and then distributed to manufacturers in that part of Ontario ? If my information is correct, 1 think very little.

My hon. friend is somewhat mistaken. The road was only completed this season to Ingersoll. My hon. friend must know that the improvements to the harbour are not completed yet. To do this business properly this company had to have a harbour on this side of the lake, they had to put on large boats to establish the coal trade. He asks me to say whether they have made a success of the coal trade. 1 am only able to give the reasons that were given to me. First, the water is not deep enough, not-withstandinig that over $100,000 have been spent on that port; secondly, the coal mines are controlled by the American railways. The coal this road will bring would come from another district altogether. They would not ship their coal in that way, but Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
