they send it round by Buffalo. For some time they did carry coal that way for the use of the railroad companies. They are supplying coal at Port Burwell from a different district on the other side from that which it was originally intended to connect with the Grand Trunk at Port Dover.

The wording of this resolution is not such as to meet my approval, even were I in favour of subsidizing a road through this country. This is one of the roads that I would not consider meritorious. It runs through a rich agricultural country from Lake Erie to Georgian bay, and passes through large manufacturing towns. If any railway can be constructed and made self-sustaining without government aid, it is surely this road. The country through which this road passes would be able to afford abundance of traffic and enable its promoters to pay dividends. However, we have already, in a resolution that we have adopted, granted a subsidy to this road from Ingersoll to Woodstock. That we have disposed of. That is not before us now. Now, we are asked to grant a further subsidy :
For a line of railway from Woodstock northerly to a point on the Grand Trunk Railway at Berlin.
That is one proposition. The other proposition is to go back to Ingersoll and grant a subsidy :
From Ingersoll to Stratford, or to any point on the Grand Trunk Railway between these places.
Or between Stratford and Berlin. It seems to me that a roving commission like this is not altogether what I may call fair-play. This company will be able to go to the city of Stratford, and say : We have a subsidy granted from Ingersoll to Stratford. If you elect a representative in North Perth to support the government the road will be conducted along that route, because we understand from the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir Wm. Mulock), in his categorical examination of my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), that the purport of these bonuses is largely to secure political support. If the city of Stratford does not concede what the promoter, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) desires, or what the government desires, and if they do not grant a municipal bonus the company are in a position to go elsewhere. They may say : We will go to Woodstock and see what they are prepared to do. If Woodstock gives a good municipal bonus in support of this road they will run the road from Ingersoll to Woodstock and thence to Berlin, providing that Berlin will grant a bonus and representati- es in favour of the government are elected in North and South Waterloo. The roving commission that this subsidy gives to this company is such as is utterly unfair to the various counties through which the road passes, because it

simply places power in the hands of the company which no railway company should be given. We have gone as far as Woodstock with the subsidy. The road is built to Ingersoll. Let the road continue from Iu-gersoll to Woodstock. I think that is the proper route. Then from Woodstock let it go north to Berlin, passing possibly through Galt, and on north from Berlin through a section of the country that is not now supplied with railway facilities, towards Collingwood. If you subsidize this road allowing it to be constructed from Ingersoll to Stratford, and' thence from Stratford northward, you are simply paralleling another road which runs to the Georgian bay. You can get on a railway train at Stratford and. go direct to Wiarton or Owen Sound. Why should we subsidize a road paralleling that existing road ? Surely the government are not so pTofuse of money that they can afford to subsidize one railway to parallel another through a well settled country such as the counties of Perth, Huron, Bruce and Grey. I do not think it is called for. I think the other is the proper route.
If you go ihe other way, you are paralleling the two roads to Woodstock direct.

I admit that, but it would only be for a distance of about nine miles. These two roads are practically through roads. Any one living near these two roads may see the trains go past upon them at a very high rate of speed. They make stops at large places. These two roads are not local roads, and as far as the distance between Woodstock and Berlin is concerned, they are practically through roads. The conditions are the same as those in the Niagara peninsula. When you I go across the Niagara peninsula you are bound to parallel other roads, because the peninsula is so narrow. Still if you want to reach the United States you have to parallel roads, but in this case you would only be obliged to parallel existing roads for a distance of about nine miles. The moment you strike Woodstock you have an opportunity of going north towards Berlin.
I dare say you will pass through such towns as Berlin, Hespeler, Galt and Waterloo, and thence on to Collingwood, so that the road will go through a country which abounds in manufacturing towns which would require the coal that the railway could supply them with. I think this bonus ought to be limited to one route, and that no roving commission should be granted. I do not think it is fair that the different municipalities should be placed in opposition to one another, or that one should be held up against the other, so that whichever bids .the highest in the shape of a municipal bonus will get the road, or that the constituency which elects a representative of a certain stripe of politics will get the road. I think that the government should lay down a certain line. Let this committee amend
this resolution in the way which I suggest.
It would be an absurd thing to parallel a road which already runs to the Georgian bay rather than going to Woodstock, where we have already given a bonus, because we have already granted a subsidy from Ingersoll to Woodstock. Bet us continue the road from Woodstock north and go through the important towns to which I have referred on the way to the Georgian bay.

It would appear that my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) does not understand the geography of the country very well, because he says that if you go from Stratford north to the Georgian bay you would be paralleling another road. You are not paralleling another road. There is no road being paralleled by going from Stratford, but if you go to Woodstock and then back to Galt, you would make a snake fence of it and'render the project impracticable. The proposition would be neither feasible nor useful. I understand that my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) desires, with the permission of the committee, to withdraw the resolution that he proposed.
I withdraw the resolution.

I am very much in sympathy with my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) in the general sentiments that he expresses, and I shall make representations to the company by telegram acquainting them with the views which have been expressed, so that we may amend the resolution before the third reading. I can assure the committee that there is no localism about this matter. It was on the representations of the company, who had obtained a charter from In-gersoll to Woodstock, that the route was described in the way in which it appears here. As the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) points out, the hon. member for Holton (Mr. Henderson) is rather mistaken as to the conditions which at present exist. There are turn first-class roads between Woodstock and Ingersoll. Besides that, there is a first-class electric road, the cars upon which go up and down every half hour, so that there is no object from the local standpoint in adopting the route which is here proposed. I think the idea of the company was that they should be in a position to adopt whichever their survey showed to be the better route. I had no idea whatever that there was any desire on the part of the company to hold up the municipalities, because these municipalities are so well supplied with railways that they could not. as a matter of fact, be held up. It never occurred to me that there was any such idea in the mind of anybody. These counties are so well supplied with railway facilities that it would be impossible to get anything like a unanimous vote in the eom-nninitv on the question. The resolution was only drawn in this way because the company asked it with the view of selecting the

best and shortest route as disclosed by tbe survey.
That portion of the road between Ingersoll and Tilsonburg would not be immediately paralleling any line, excepting for a few miles.
You mean from Ingersoll to Stratford.
Yes, from In-gersoll to Stratford.
There is a splendid country there.

There is a good country there, and if it ran directly from Stratford to Collingwood it would not parallel any road. But I do not think that a road to Woodstock should be bonused as there are already three roads there.
This has been voted for some years.

Then to go from Woodstock to either Galt or Guelph, as has been said, would be to make a snake fence of it. I can certainly see very serious objection to the way this bonus is given; it is encouraging each town to vote a bonus to the railway. I think the minister should either hold this over, or word it so as to remove the objectionable features.

I beg to move that all the words after the word ' from ' in the second line be struck out and the following be substituted therefor
' Ingersoll towards Collingwood in the most direct and practicable route not exceeding 35 miles.'
I think that gives a starting point with the other objective point at Collingwood.

We might let this stand until we hear from * the company any objections they may have to that wording; personally I have no objection to it.
To the Irondale, Bancroft and Ottawa Railway Company for a line of railway from the present terminus of its railway, near Bancroft, easterly to a point at or near Renfrew, not exceeding seventy-five miles.

With reference to tliis resolution with respect to tbe Irondale and Bancroft road I would say that *this aid has been pressed upon this government by a number of municipalities, including the city of Toronto, the town of Lindsay, the Board of Trade of the city of Ottawa. the Board of Trade of Lindsay, and the Board of Trade of Renfrew. Various other municipalities have pressed this upon the government, but as some sort of objection to it seeems to be manifested I would suggest that it stand over till to-morrow. I may inform my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) that my object in doing this with reference to this and tbe James bay resolution, which is farther down on the Order I Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
Paper, is that perhaps my hon. friend would like to take advantage of the presence here to-morrow of a deputation from the Toronto city council. Perhaps he desires to consult them with regard to these two subsidies. I can assure him that they have been pressed upon us very strongly by the city of Toronto. If tbe bon. gentleman desires it I would suggest that they stand over until that deputation arrives.

Anything the city of Toronto could have to say about this would be well said, and I am sure that tbe hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) will not object to it because it is carrying out Ills policy of opening up a new district and when completed it will give to the city of Toronto another through line to the city of Ottawa. This road was pressed forward for a number of years by Mr. Pusey, who came in here giving his time and energy to this project and he fought an up hill fight such as few men in Canada have fought and succeeded in building the road a considerable distance. Mi-. Howland is now managing tbe road to tbe best of bis ability. It opens up a country which is somewhat rugged but one which I am sure will be in a few years rich in mining. The famous corundum mines were opened up owing to the fact of this railway bringing settlers to the region. I would like to see this vote passed.

The objection to this proposed vote would be that it is diverting the line from the route originally intended. Mr. Pusey did not intend to go to Renfrew but to make connection with the road from Brockville to Westport. It was his intention to work down in that direction and as evidence of that he commenced to build a bridge from Brockville across the St. Lawi'ence. You will see there one or two of tbe piers partly built and there should be some serious reason why the road is being diverted from its original line towards Renfrew.

The original intention was to build the road to Ottawa. It starts from ICinmount and runs through Irondale and Bancroft, so that this is returning to the original intention. Some years later when the Brockville and Westport railway got into difficulties, Mr. Pusey abandoned the original route and intended to divert the road to connect with the Brockville and Westport, intending to cross the St. Lawrence at Brockville and to have a through route to the west.' I know his intentions because I had the privilege of being consulted by him in every move he made. That scheme has been dropped for a number of years past and the intention has been to make a connection with Ottawa, in other words to go back to the original intention of the projector of the railway.

This road has been built a distance of forty-five or fifty miles and

bus received and earned government aid. It has now been bonused by the Ontario government for a distance of seventy-five miles at $3,000 a mile, and we expect to get assistance from this government and then the road will be completed because financial arrangements have been made with the Knickerbocker Company of New York to complete it. With reference to the possibilities of this road you must understand that with the Madawaska river near where the York branch unites there is situated one of the finest corundum mines in the world. They are spending this year nearly a quarter of a million dollars and this mine will practically control the corundum market of the world. For the information of the House I would like to lay upon the Table a picture of this Corundum mine, also a cut of the buildings, which are now being erected and which along with the machinery will cost as I said a quarter of a million dollars.
I would also like to submit a sample of the corundum crystal which perhaps none of you have ever seen and also some of the manufactured article. It is an abrasive mineral and the samples which 1 show you embrace the finest and also the coarsest grades, from No. 12 to No. 200. We expect that they will do an immense business in corundum which is wanted in every iron manufacturing establishment in the world. The company are now shipping their produce all over Canada, carloads are being sent to the great manufactories in the United States and the corundum is also being shipped in great quantities to Great Britain and other countries of Europe. The great difficulty hitherto has been that the road was so far from any railway that the cost of shipping these goods has been almost prohibitive. But you must bear in mind that this corundum mine is not the only mine in this country that this railway will open up.
If you go about twenty-five miles further down the Madawaska, you come to the finest molybdenite mine in the world. This mineral is so extensive that one of the farmers has actually fenced his whole farm with it. It is used in the manufacture of the very highest grade of steel. This mine, which is already started, will be put in such a shape that this material can be shipped, and it will be of inestimable value to this country. In the same vicinity there have been opened up magnificent iron ' mines of . the highest grade of ore for the manufacture of steel. So you have these two elements lying side by side. The difficulty at present is that the ore has to be drawn thirty or forty miles, and it is almost impossible to do it. If this road is built, it will be possible to ship that ore. Twelve miles still further down the river, in the township of Brougham, you come to the Ontario Graphite Company's mine, one of the finest mines in the Dominion of Canada. This company has already spent about $75,000 in opening up this mine. Only last week
they shipped a carload of manufactured goods to Berlin in Germany. Those who visited the Pan-American Exposition must have seen the magnificent exhibit of this company there. Theirs is the only mine of its kind now being operated anywhere in the Dominion of Canada. The material is of the highest grade. The Ontario government has purchased the exhibit which was at the Pan-American for the purpose of sending it to the St. Louis Expositiofi^ next year. In view of the prospects of this railway in opening up all these magnificent mines, I cannot understand why anybody should oppose this grant.

In reply to the remarks of the Postmaster General in regard to this Bancroft Railway, I would like the House to understand that I am not an opponent of granting assistance to every railway, but I am oposed to granting public money to undesirable railways. Not only do I support a grant to this particular railway, but I have put a large amount of money into it myself. That money has been sunk for several years, and I shall not get a cent of it back again. Therefore I am not selfish in supporting or opposing any particular railway. With regard to the veiled threat which the hon. gentleman has thrown across to me, that I may meet some citizens of Toronto who are coming here, and may delight his heart by getting up a wrangle with them, he need not be alarmed. They know my opinions. I may not be a municipal officer coming down here to urge the interests of any railway company ; I represent the city of Toronto, and I am positively opposed to the granting of subsidies to railways through well settled parts of the country, particularly when those railways are going to parallel others. I have supported one from a harbour on Lake Erie, where we are spending a, large amount of money, for the purpose of having coal brought into this country more cheaply than it is now. But the Postmaster General need not fancy for one moment that I object to meet people with whom I have lived all my life, even though it should be in a committee on a matter of this kind. I am anxious to promote the welfare of this country, and I believe that in opposinig the granting of bonuses in the omnibus way in which they are being put through this House, I am acting in the best interests of this country.

I do not think that the delegation from the city of Toronto are coming here to-morrow in the interests of any railway company, as the hon. gentleman seems to suggest. The only reason that I know of why they are coming is contained in a telegram which I received from the head of the city, stating that they were coming down to urge the government and parliament to acquiesee in an amendment made by the Senate to the Railway Commission Bill.
Why should you invite me to meet them on that account ?

1 do not ask the hon. gentleman to take any course. But when in the early part of this discussion he expressed himself so strongly against railway bonuses generally, I told him that he would not oppose certain bonuses in this list, and now I am sustained in that view. I understand that he acquiesces in the bonus to the Bancroft Railway. I told him that I thought he would consider that a good bonus.
X want to use common sense.

X am glad to hear it ; and since the hon. gentleman expresses himself in favour of this bonus, X have no desire to postpone the consideration of it. We put it in the list because this was pressed upon us as a meritorious enterprise. The road will open up a country rich not only in minerals, but in agriculture, and will ultimately connect the west with the Ottawa district. The bonus has been pressed on the government by the city of Toronto, the city of Ottawa, the town of Lindsay, the town of Renfrew, and all the municipalities through which the line will pass. Several deputations from these municipalities have waited on the government, and have represented that the railway will open up and develop valuable resources in the district to be served. So that it would seem to be a very useful road, and I am glad to know that our action in aiding it has the unanimous approval apparently of hon. gentlemen of this committee.
To the Nepigon Railway Company, for a line of railway from Lake Superior to Lake Nepigon, and from a point on the north shore of Lake Nepigon northerly, not exceeding eighty miles.
Where is that railway expected to go ?

It is proposed to be built from Lake Superior to Lake Nepigon, about forty miles Then, I understand that Lake Nepigon is about 100 miles long; and I believe the idea is to connect the lake with a through line.

Will the minister explain where the Grand Trunk Pacific is to come in ? Only a short time ago we saw some' gentlemen down here doing some engineering, and the next day we saw an item to the effect that the Grand Trunk Pacific was going to run a branch to Nepigon bay. This railway is to go there too. Is it the intention to have two railways from Nepigon north ?
This would hardly serve that purpose. There is a large territory there which has no railway at all.
It never will have.

My hon. friend is mistaken. There is a splendid country there, with plenty of resources. I am not able to tell you the location of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but I hope that some day or other there will be one or two roads running through there, and this may connect with it.
Is there a charter for this road across Lake Nepigon ?
I think the scheme is to build from Lake Superior to Lake Nepigon, and then from Lake Nepigon about 40 miles north.
Is not the charter for a continuous railway?
Yes.

Why not build around the lake. To build a road up to Lake Nepigon and then take a canoe or steamer across the lake, and then build a railway on, would be nonsense. A road that will go around the lake will have to keep a slight distance to the west, and there you would get a very good valley.

The
road will be forty miles to Lake Nepigon, and I think it is eighty miles from the south to the north of Lake Nepigon. Then the road will be forty miles nox-th from Lake Nepigon, or eighty miles of railway or thereabouts plus the navigable waters of the lake, which will furnish communications between the outside world and the Grand Trunk Pacific in the course of construction, and provide means of getting in supplies and material. Perhaps later on the owners may connect the two pieces.
Is this to be a colonization road ?

For the present it will certainly be, pure and simple, because after building from Lake Superior to Lake Nepigon. they propose to use the lake, which is between 90 and 100 miles long. It is represented that * there ai'e large pulpwood limits there, and it is intended to establish there pulp and fishing industries. The parties are putting their own money into it, and are prepared to build next season if they receive assistance.

I understand that the object is to construct a road from a point on the Canadian Pacific Railway to Lake Nepigon, but I understand that that road has also a subsidy from the Ontario gov-ei-nment for the first ten miles. Then they are supposed to navigate Lake Nepigon for the purpose of bringing up pulpwood and other material down, and it is to be a colonization road as well.
Those are the representations made to me.
It can only be a summer road. In the winter time the lake is not navigable.

The road will be used in the winter time for taking in supplies and you can drive across the lake.
To the Manitoulin and North Shore Railway Company for a line of railway from Little Current. on its present line, to Sudbury and thenoe towards the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, not exceeding thirty miles, in lieu of the subsidy of twenty-one miles granted by chapter 7 of 1899, item 38 of section 2.
This is a revote of 21 miles and nine miles new. It is to run into the nickel mines and will connect with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Is that ultimately supposed to go to James' bay ?
No, the Manitoulin and North Shore line runs south of the Canadian Pacific Railway across the Manitoulin islands. Its charter carries it back to Ontario.
Is this part of the Clergue system of railway, bonused already by the Ontario government and for which we voted a bonus before ?
Yes.

This is part of the railway that was to go down to Manitoulin across to Tobermory and further down by Wiarton and from Wiarton to Meaford. I said some years ago that I never believed it was seriously intended to build the Manitoulin part of it. However, Mr. Clergue was ingenious enough to get nearly all southwestern Ontario to join with him in an application for a subsidy to build this railway, and the bonuses he got he used in order to build back -into the woods to his own pulp lands and mines. I would be much better pleased if this had been spent for the purpose of building the Manitoulin part down to Tobermory and from there by way of Wiarton to Meaford. That would have given us a short road across that section to the Soo, to the Canadian Pacific Railway, but I imagine this must be dropped. Who is behind this now ?

My hon. friend is somewhat mistaken as to the roads. Mr. Clergue and those associated with him had two charters-one the Manitoulin and North Shore and the other the Algoma Central. They were granted subsidies by parliament for both roads, but there are some twenty-one miles on which the subsidies are still good for another year, granted to the Manitoulin and North Shore Company. The subsidy Mr. Clergue used
on the Algoma Central, which he built up to the mines and north towards the Canadian Pacific Railway. That was a different organization, although under the control of Mr. Clergue and his associates.
' But this road was to go to Little Current and from therel to extend on to the Canadian Pacific Railway.

However, there are two separate oragniza-tions. Mr. Clergue has built more of the Algoma Central-a hundred and odd miles- and of this only twelve or thirteen miles starting from Sudbury and running out into the mining country ; and this nine miles extension is in a different direction and was not subsidized before. We will admit that the enterprises with which Mr. Clergue was associated are not at the moment successful. Still, many of us would regard them as great undertakings, and we all must admit that he has succeeded in spending a great deal of money in that district. No doubt those enterprises are in difficulties by all reports, but I have still confidence that many of these industries will be established and become successful. And he represents that he has still the expectation

	.
Who represents ?

Mr. Clergue. He is, so far as I know the representative of these railway propositions. He says he has financial arrangements pending to put these roads through, if he is given the support. He has done wonderful things in the past, and it seems to me we might take the risk of this small renewal. We want to see the road built, there is no doubt about that. A great deal of money has been spent in that district, and, for my par,t, I have still confidence that many of the industries will be carried on there. And I hope that Mr. Clergue will reap some reward for the work he has done and the enterprise he has shown. The first investors in some of these industries may lose. We shall be sorry if that is the case, but I believe that the country will be developed and many of these enterprises will be successful in the end.

I believe that too. But I must say that I think Mr. Clergue is considerable of a fakir in railway promoting. That is my opinion from the experience we have had of -him so far. He is an able man no doubt. He has started many industries which, if continued, will be of a most valuable character, and I am sure every one will be glad to see him rewarded for his enterprise. But I think his greatest cause of failure is that, as soon as he starts one, enterprise, instead of prosecuting it to successful end, he branches out into something else in which he sees millions, follows "it a certain distance, starts something else and so on. With re-

gard to bis railway schemes, let me give the committee an idea of them. He got western Ontario to support his scheme for a bonus. He was going to build from Mea-ford up to Tobermory, reach Manitoulin, cross to Little Current, thence to the north shore and so north. This scheme his friends used two or three times during the elections. In North Grey he had the announcement made in the ' Monitor ' calling for the building of the whole road. I had left Ottawa, but a short time before, and, up to that time, he had not his plans filed with the, government when the statement was made" that he was calling for tenders for the construction of the road. I wrote to Ottawa to ask if he had his plans filed then, and the answer I received was that no maps or plans had been filed. Yet, though he had not laid his plans before the government or received their consent, be called for tenders for the building of the whole road, seeking to convince the people that the road was to be built at once. After the election was) over, of course, there was a quietus for a time. There was a protest, the sitting member was unseated and a new election was called. Then, the same game was gone over with. It served the same purpose two or three times, and I do not know how many more times it will be used. I am satisfied there was no serious intention of commencing the road. Yet, Mr. Clergue sent out surveyors, of two different routes. Those people who wanted the road to go by the north route were told to support the government candidate and they would get what they wanted ; and those who wanted the south route were told the same thing. We would not have complained so much about all this had he gone on and built the railway. But the aim seems to be the same as from the first. He mapped out a large scheme to secure support from a large number of municipalities, including towns and cities, so as to secure a bonus to enable him to complete that portion of the railway back into his mining and pulpwood areas, and he has used that for the purpose of building' back in that direction. I do not say this is objectionable, for even the building of that road would be valuable ; but he has led a lot of people into the belief that he seriously intended to build the Manitoulin and North Shore, which I do not think he ever did. Now, we are proposing to give him a little help, for his railway back into the mining district. If he seriously intends to build it and will prosecute it,
I do not say that it is objectionable, because it would do good to the locality.
Would not this pass near the Spanish River Pulp Company, and their large works going on at the present time ?

Yes, they have a mile and a half built from the Canadian Pacific Mr. SPROULE.
Railway to the Spanish River Pulp Company.

I desire to make a suggestion. It is hardly likely that we can pass all these items to-night. When charters are applied for large maps are brought before the Railway Committee, showing where the road is to be built, the location of parallel roads, and so on. Would it be possible for the department, in view of these bonuses, to have these maps laid before the Committee of the Whole ? In that way we could have a better idea of the situation than we can have from the small maps. For myself, I am very much at sea without this information, and I think a great many of us are in the same position.
Of course the charters of some of the roads to be subsidized were passed, not this session, but years ago. The maps may not be available. But, any that are available I will endeavour to bring down.

Surely there must be something very wrong in the wording of this resolution. It is not intelligible to me. It says :
To the Manitoulin and North Shore Railway Company for a line of railway from Little Current, on its present line, to Sudbury, and thence towards the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
When you are at Sudbury you are on the main line.
I have just had my attention drawn to that. It does seem somewhat unintelligible.

This is being asked for by the solicitor of the company, and, I suppose, it is put in as he worded it. It would be as well, perhaps, to have it looked into to learn what the explanation is. Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) have any objection to this being passed, with the understanding that it would be explained or amended on the third reading ?
I object to the passing of it on general principles.

But now that the hon. gentleman's conscience is eased, and he knows that these votes are going through anyway, I would suggest that it is hardly worth while holding over a small item like this when we can pass it with the understanding that on the third reading it can be passed or explained.

That is, give the government a roving commission to change the resolution, and they might make it apply to a railway to run to the moon. I would not like to say I would vote for a subsidy and leave it to the government
Very well, let the item stand!

What the Minister of Public Works means is that when the Bill comes to its final stage in committee, we can make the correction, That is what my hon. friend proposes, not that the government should make it.
To the Thunder Bay, Nepigon and St. Joe Railway Company for a line of railway from Port Arthur north-easterly, not exceeding fifty miles.

This road will pass through a good farming district. I think Mr. Burke, of Port Arthur, is the leading promoter. We have telegrams from a number of representative persons in that neighbourhood asking for this subsidy. I have an application from the Board of Trade of Port Arthur in support of this subsidy.
What subsidy or bonus has the provincial government given to this road ?
$2,000 a mile.

$2,000 in cash subsidy is given for the first 10 miles and a land grant of 5,000 acres per mile for the whole distance of 225 miles. Is this subsidy to be applied on the first 10 miles, for which the cash subsidy is given by the province of Ontario ?

The information furnished to me does not state the number of miles. It states the government of Ontario have granted a subsidy, and I presume that our subsidy will cover the same mileage as far as it goes.

I am afraid we cannot agree to abandon any part of that excellent scheme.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.

Would the hon. Minister
of Finance tell us what business we will take up to-morrow ?
There are some Bills and orders standing on the Paper which we desire to take up which will not likely occupy much time, and then we will proceed with the railway subsidies.
Would the hon. minister state when we may expect the resolution in regard to the Quebec bridge ?

My hon. friend will find that on the notice paper in the morning. It was sent upstairs some time ago, and it will appear in the Votes
and Proceedings in the morning.
Have the government any further information to convey to the House relating to the Alaskan boundary ? It was announced that they would likely come to' a decision this afternoon or tomorrow.
While it is Tuesday in London, it is hardly Tuesday here. We have no official information to give to my hon. friend.
